cards.title: Everyday Uncertainty: How Blind People Use GenAI Tools for Information Access

rows.value: other
primary empirical, concept or theory, failure or counterevidence

Twenty blind screen reader users, interviewed for an hour each, plus logged sessions from a blind co-author. The finding that transfers is what these users do with a tool they know is wrong a lot of the time: they stop asking it for answers. One participant reports that roughly half the links Gemini gives him are wrong or dead and uses it anyway, for the keywords - 'If I don't use AI, I'm not sure what the keywords would be.' Another takes ChatGPT's outline of a paper and then reads the paper, 'because I don't totally believe it'. The support is deliberately confined to ground where the user can already catch it: one uses it only on tasks where he has 'a clue about the output', another 'never use[s] it for anything important', a third 'won't hang a life on' its descriptions. And verification itself fails twice in the data. A sighted professional interpreter agreed with an AI description of hands on a braille book that turned out to be candy buttons, which the authors say 'call[s] into question what constitutes verification and correctness'. The co-author tested Be My AI for consistency by toggling a radiator's buttons and re-prompting, was satisfied, and only learned from his partner that the descriptions never matched the scene at all - a turning point after which he could not '100% trust the result'. The paper's recommendation is to stop evaluating models on isolated, time-bounded tasks and to support the person's ongoing reasoning instead.

medium · A carefully conducted interview study whose evidence is entirely self-report, and which makes no claim otherwise. Twenty blind screen reader users recruited through academic networks, the American Foundation for the Blind and snowball sampling, one hour each, reflexive thematic analysis with coding by the lead author discussed with the team, informed by an initial analysis of a blind co-author's own logged sessions with three tools. A positionality statement is given. What bounds it: nothing is measured, counted or compared. The claims are patterns across accounts, usually supported by two to seven named participants, and the two strongest incidents - the interpreter who agreed with a wrong description, and the radiator panel - are single cases, one of them recounted second-hand from a post the participant read online. All participants are US-based, English-speaking, recruited partly through professional networks, and self-selected for existing GenAI use, so this is a sample of skilled and reflective adopters rather than of blind people generally. Read it for the mechanisms and the vocabulary, not for prevalence.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A support known to be unreliable is not necessarily either trusted or abandoned; it can be reassigned to a job its unreliability cannot spoil. That is the mechanism this paper documents and it is worth carrying into the whole AI cluster. Half of P5's links are wrong or dead, so he stops taking links and takes vocabulary - the one thing a model that has misremembered the documents can still supply, since knowing what a field calls something does not require the citations to exist. P2 stops taking the summary as content and takes it as an index, then reads the source. P9 uses the tool only for the one operation he has found it reliable at, reporting which snippet a pointer highlights. In each case what changes is not the model's accuracy and not whether the support is present, but how much of the task is delegated to it - narrowed until the residual error rate stops mattering. Two things follow for a review of supports. First, this is a fourth response to an unreliable support alongside trust, rejection and verification, and it is invisible to any evaluation that measures whether the output was correct. Second, the narrowing is done by the user, not the designer, and requires them to have discovered what the tool is dependably good at.

(PDF p. 6) The shift from verifying output to using it — The central behavioural finding: working with hallucinations and error-prone output was an assumed part of using these tools, and use shifted from simply verifying output to skilfully making use of error-prone output - developing a tolerance for certain kinds of error and integrating the tools into situated workflows such as reasoning where contextual cues are rich, extracting outlines to aid document reading, and identifying terminology before searching.
quotes: Our findings extend this prior work, as we found that working with model hallucinations, or otherwise error-prone output, was often an assumed part of using GenAI tools for access among our participants. Their use shifted from simply verifying output to skillfully making use of error-prone output as part of information access. They developed a tolerance for certain kinds of errors, learning to integrate error-prone GenAI tools into their sit­ uated practices and workflows, such as reasoning in environments with rich contextual cues (e.g., personal photos, or physical objects, in both digital and physical environments), extracting outlines to facilitate document reading, and identifying terminology before conducting an online search

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) Half the links are wrong and the tool is still useful — The clearest case of using a tool through its error rate: P5 estimates that half the links Gemini gives him are wrong or dead, and uses it anyway for the keywords to put into Google, because without the AI he would not know what the keywords were - and because on a search results page every item has to be judged for reliability, which is expensive with a screen reader.
quotes: P5, for instance, shared how he gathered keywords from erroneous output to help narrow down and focus his web search. “Sometimes I ask Gemini to summarize, for example, the U.S. national strategy on a certain thing. It sounds ridiculous, right?...Gemini would see a lot of things and it’ll probably mention a few documents. It may even provide some links. I think 50% of the links are either wrong or dead...(However,) I get a very nice bunch of keywords, and I can put the things into Google. If I don’t use AI, I’m not sure what the keywords would be.” In this example, he was not turning to search engines for verification [4], but instead, he assumed errors in the output and shifted focus to information that he could use to narrow down his search space. The advantage of Gemini’s summarizing ability is evident for him as a screen reader user as opposed to search engines, because “for every item on the web page, you have to verify, like if this source is reliable or not, or if this title is interesting or not. A lot of judgments came in

rows.value: (PDF p. 6) The outline as a navigation aid, read anyway — The outline as a navigation aid rather than an answer: five participants used GenAI to extract a rough document structure to know what to attend to, with P2 saying that every time after the summarisation he reads the article because he does not totally believe it.
quotes: While GenAI models are far from perfect in summarizing long documents [44], participants found it useful to generate a rough structure to help them preview content and know what to attend to when reading. P2 and P8 shared that, before using ChatGPT, they frequently needed to read through substantial portions of a paper to understand the structure, even when they were generally familiar with common paper structures. P2’s experience represented a typical reading experience with ChatGPT or similar text-based GenAI tools. “I’ll have a rough understanding of the structure of the article, the main view, and the key points [with the outline GPT generated]. I know there may be three main points in the article’s main body, and I will know when it comes to the first one.” He emphasized that “every time after the summarization, I’ll read the article because I don’t totally believe it.” In this example, P2 fully expected the possibility of AI hallucination, and thus he only sought a structured

rows.value: (PDF p. 6) Errors that do not matter, and errors you can anticipate — Two worked cases: P2 found that models rarely err on high-level structure or object category, so misrecognising one kind of tree as another does not affect his purpose of sorting photos of scenery from photos of people; and P9, an accessibility engineer, uses Picture Smart AI on client screenshots because it reliably reports which code snippet a pointer is highlighting.
quotes: When we asked P2 how he dealt with AI halluci­ nation in image description, he told us based on his experience the AI models he used usually do not make mistakes in terms of high-level image structures or categories of the objects. As such, he developed a way to use AI for selecting photos for his online sharing because “misrecognizing a palm tree into another type of tree wouldn’t affect” as long as he gets the cues to know if it is a photo of scenery or people. As another example, P9, who worked as an accessibility engineer, often used Picture Smart AI to check screenshots of test cases provided by his client. While the output was expected to have errors, his work experience equipped him with certain anticipations toward the output. As he said, “Typically in the screenshots there’ll be a highlight or pointer, pointing at the code in question. And usually, AI is able to tell something like the focus or whatever they’re using to point to this code snippet. Tell me what code snippets are being focused or emphasized

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) Verification as ongoing rather than one-time — Incompleteness as distinct from error: rather than seeing verification as a one-time task, participants treated all information and understanding as tentative, gradually refining their grasp of both the subject and the tools.
quotes: The experience of everyday uncertainty is also reflected in partici­ pants’ sense of incompleteness in using AI for access. In contrast to errors and hallucinations, the sense of incompleteness arises from the richness of the information itself, combined with the opaque and ever-evolving nature of GenAI models. Consequently, rather than seeing verification as a one-time task, participants treated all information and understanding as tentative, gradually refining their understanding of both the information they were exploring and the tools used in their process

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The users keep the tool off the ground where they could not catch it, and they say so in almost those words. Only where you have a clue about the output; never for anything important; not where a life hangs on it. P15 caught the mac and cheese because he knew what he had bought - the check came from his own prior knowledge of the situation, not from anything the system offered. This is the accessibility cluster's version of a pattern the corpus has now seen in software engineering and in music: the ability to check the machine tracks the very knowledge the machine is meant to supply, so the support is safest exactly where it is least needed and riskiest where it would help most. What is distinctive here is that the users have already worked this out and imposed the boundary on themselves, at a cost: the high-stakes, low-knowledge situations - the ones where inaccessible information matters most - are the ones they decline to use the tool for. Note also what the boundary is not. It is not a designed restriction, nothing in these applications models what the user knows, and no tool in the study asks whether this is a domain the person can check.

rows.value: Additionally, he told us, out of concerns about AI hallucinations, he would only use GenAI tools on tasks where he had a clue about the output like the workplace screenshots. quotes: Similarly, participants drew on knowledge of their local material environment to extract meaningful cues from erroneous outputs related to physical objects (P9, P11, P13, P15, P17). items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: Two incidents in one paper show verification failing from both directions, and together they are the sharpest thing in this cluster about what checking can and cannot do. In the first, the checker is a trained human professional, entirely outside the model, and he agrees with a description that is wrong; independence of the verifier did not help, because both were looking at the same image with the same prior expectation, and the error only surfaced when the picture reached a wider group. In the second, the check is a serious, well-designed test run from inside the arrangement: the co-author physically toggled the radiator's buttons and re-prompted to see whether the tool tracked the change and stayed consistent. It passed. The descriptions were fabricated throughout - an unlit power button reported as green - and this only came out through his partner. A consistency test cannot detect an error the system makes consistently, which is the same in-system versus independent conflict the corpus has recorded in tutoring research, arriving here as a lived incident. The practical rule to carry: a verification step inherits the blind spots of whatever it shares with the thing being verified, whether that is a model, a modality or an expectation.

rows.value: 'The Aira agent agreed that the AI's description was correct, but it turned out to be misleading when I shared it on my group. quotes: In one case, our member researcher kept checking his understanding and Be My AI’s reliability when he asked the application to describe a radiator panel. He turned on/off the buttons on the panels several times, and kept modifying his prompts to see if Be My AI could capture the change and if it was consistent in outputs. However, later when he checked with his partner, he realized that Be My AI kept providing details that did not match the actual scene (e.g., stating the power button was green when it had no light). This moment became a “turning point” for him. He found that he could not “100% trust the result

quotes: However, not all instances of subjectivity are desirable, making contending with subjectivity a routine experience for access. Par­ ticipants cited the “cheesy” descriptions AI tools generated, such as always describing a room as “beautiful” or a sofa as “cozy” regard­ less of the actual scene or object in question (P7, P9, P10, P11, P12, P14, P16). P16 provided an example, “when I was outside, walking in my backyard, sometimes it describes things as lush and breathtaking. They might not be all that incredible.” While the partiality in this example might be perceived as obvious, other instances are more subtle and difficult to detect. For example, ordinary clothing in one culture might be perceived as costume-like in another (P12). As a result, participants raised concerns that the partiality of infor­ mation creates perpetual uncertainty with using GenAI for access, particularly when the information carries criticality. The radiator panel is the mirror case: the co-author ran a genuine consistency test from inside the arrangement, toggling the hardware and re-prompting, and passed it, while the descriptions were fabricated throughout. items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The support does not sit beside the person; it rearranges who else is in the room and what each of them does. Three movements are visible. It displaces human help - one participant reports calling volunteers far less often - and the displacement is partly welcome, since the paper's own related work records that poor human assistance can undermine a person's sense of independence and make them hesitant to ask. It raises the cost of returning to human help, because switching from a model to a stranger carries social and cognitive demands and feels wasteful after time invested in the AI - a switching cost the corpus has not previously recorded, and one that will bias any observed usage pattern toward whichever source was tried first. And in the best case it inverts the direction of help: after having the model restate a recipe in his own terms, the co-author's wife followed his instructions rather than the reverse, and he reports feeling more engaged and involved. That last one matters for a review of supports because it is an outcome no measure of output quality can see. The syrup was not better. What changed is who held the plan - a redistribution of role inside a joint activity, achieved by the support arriving on the side of the person who usually receives help rather than on the side of the person who usually gives it.

rows.value: 'Be My AI drastically cut down the amount that I've had to call a volunteer'... participants typically expressed concerns about the variance of assistance quality and the socio-cognitive demands involved in the transition from a GenAI model to a random person, especially after investing time and efforts into using AI... 'when my wife was helping me, making that rosemary syrup, she was following my instructions because I knew all the steps, because I asked GPT to summarize it in my way of understanding.' In these instances, the availability of GenAI tools shifted the power dynamics of what each person contributed to a collaborative task, making the researcher feel 'more engaged and involved in the conversations.'

quotes: Given the inherent subjectivity in information access among AI and humans, participants described intentionally choosing certain sources according to perceived strengths. On the whole, participants typically found value in GenAI tools’ consistent comprehensive descriptions, which usually follow a systematic top-to-bottom, left- to-right approach (P1, P18) and setting a framework first (P5)2 . This systematic approach allowed participants to have greater access to incidental information, e.g., unexpected elements on webpages like logos (P13). Participants explained that GenAI tools could even capture visual nuances often overlooked by sighted individuals, such as a small taint on a wall, and a blurred, small bird in a photo of an airplane (P6, P16). Based on reasoning about different expertise of AI and humans, P15 described a hybrid approach to have more control over his access, “Be My AI drastically cut down the amount that I’ve had to call a volunteer to help me...I can just have my VoiceOver describe everything for me, and it’ll speak it much faster than a human. The challenges in tradeoffs were obvious in participants’ hesitation to use the volunteer option within the Be My AI application even if they were aware of the feature [95]. While many appreciate human assistance, participants typically expressed concerns about the variance of assistance qual­ ity [84] and the socio-cognitive demands involved in the transition from a GenAI model to a random person, especially after investing time and efforts into using AI (P7, P11). Others noted pervasive bias or anxiety sighted people have in helping blind people (P13, P20). For instance, P13 told us sometimes people assume she cannot do things due to age-related stereotypes (e.g., describing everything when she asked for “even the slightest amount of information”). items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The methodological half of the paper is unusually close to this review's own question, reached from accessibility rather than from learning. The diagnosis: the field evaluates models on isolated, time-bounded, de-contextualised tasks, which cannot see any of the practices the study found, because every one of them spans several tools, several sources and several occasions. The prescription has two parts, and the second is the notable one. First, evaluate inside the user's real workflow with their other tools available, and run long-term studies of effects over time. Second - and this is the part that pairs directly with the corpus's spine - move the target of improvement from the model to the person: greater certainty can come from the user's ongoing practice, reflection and communication rather than from prediction and control by a specific model, and tools could be designed to help users cultivate epistemic virtues over time. That is a proposal to build supports that make the person better at judging, which is a capability that would survive the tool. The paper does not test any of it, and it does not measure a single person: there is no task, no test, no before and after, and the one behavioural change reported is self-reported. So this is a well-argued statement of what the missing study would be, from authors who name its absence themselves.

rows.value: Accessibility research has a long history of classifying blind people's visual needs, often framing accessibility tasks as de-contextualized, isolated, and time-bounded activities... This siloed approach, however, stands in contrast to the many situated use cases our findings uncovered... we recommend that future accessibility research shift its focus from model prediction and control to supporting users in continuous engagement and reasoning... greater certainty can come from ongoing practice, reflection, and communication, rather than being solely reliant on rigid prediction and control by specific models... Additionally, tools could be designed to help users cultivate epistemic virtues over time... This calls for long-term studies that explore how GenAI tools operate within broader societal contexts and affect users' experiences over time.

(PDF p. 12) The critique of de-contextualised task design — The critique of how the field builds tasks: accessibility research has a long history of classifying visual needs and framing tasks as de-contextualised, isolated and time-bounded, with a tendency toward end-to-end solutions, which stands in contrast to the situated uses found here - extracting keywords to expand a web search, using an outline to locate places of interest, and cross-referencing descriptions when interpretation rather than verification is the goal.
quotes: Accessibility research has a long history of classifying blind people’s visual needs [21, 45], often framing accessibility tasks as de-contextualized, isolated, and time- bounded activities. Typical examples in the context of blindness include image or scene descriptions [24, 45, 92, 143, 152] and object recognition [49, 67, 100, 116, 128, 130], with a tendency to empha­ size end-to-end solutions. This siloed approach, however, stands in contrast to the many situated use cases our findings uncovered, such as expanding on web search using keywords extracted from AI output, using AI-generated outlines to locate places of interests during reading, and cross-referencing visual descriptions when interpretation, rather than verification, is the goal

rows.value: (PDF p. 12) Shift the focus from model control to the user's reasoning — The central recommendation: shift accessibility research from model prediction and control to supporting users in continuous engagement and reasoning, because greater certainty can come from ongoing practice, reflection and communication rather than from rigid prediction and control by specific models.
quotes: To center PWD’s perspectives in addressing uncertainty, we rec­ ommend that future accessibility research shift its focus from model prediction and control to supporting users in continuous engage­ ment and reasoning. This approach aligns with the established tra­ dition of sense-making and CSCW research, such as user-centered misinformation interventions [54]. In other words, greater certainty can come from ongoing practice, reflection, and communication, rather than being solely reliant on rigid prediction and control by specific models

rows.value: (PDF p. 12) Design tools that build the person's epistemic virtues — A design implication aimed at the person rather than the model: tools could be designed to help users cultivate epistemic virtues over time, for example by framing model outputs in ways that encourage skepticism.
quotes: Additionally, tools could be designed to help users cultivate epistemic virtues over time, such as framing model outputs in ways that encourage skepticism

rows.value: (PDF p. 12) Evaluate in the real workflow, and over time — The evaluation implication: evaluate models and tools in naturalistic real-world scenarios inside users' actual workflows with their other tools available, and run long-term studies of how these tools operate in broader societal contexts and affect users' experiences over time.
quotes: A crucial next step is to evaluate GenAI models and design tools in naturalistic, real-world scenarios. For example, consider how participants extracted keywords from GenAI responses to facilitate web search. Evaluations should be conducted within users’ actual search flows, ensuring that other information tools, like search engines, are easily available. Similarly, design should consider the user’s entire workspace. For instance, to optimize the search ex­ perience, tools could help users quickly identify named entities in AI responses and link them directly to relevant web search results (e.g., see recent work on interactive LLMs as potential examples [64, 124]). A thoughtful design process must also consider the po­ litical and social dynamics of real-world use. For example, model errors that could cause social embarrassment should be addressed as a priority [2]. This calls for long-term studies that explore how GenAI tools operate within broader societal contexts and affect users

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Plurality, skepticism, dissent, humility — The four epistemic dispositions the authors name - plurality, skepticism, dissent and humility - and their alignment with virtue epistemology, which shifts emphasis from the qualities of knowledge to the knower and to the intellectual virtues needed to acquire, maintain and apply knowledge over time.
quotes: As such, rather than seeking a single truth as implied by ground- truth labels [21, 150], participants’ approach to information access emphasized plurality (recognizing different ways of knowing), skep­ ticism (acknowledging potential inaccuracy, incompleteness, and bias), dissent (actively seeking alternative perspectives), and hu­ mility (accepting ignorance). These practices echo the principles of virtue epistemology, which shifts the epistemological emphasis from the qualities of knowledge to the knower, prioritizing the intellectual virtues important to acquiring, maintaining, and ap­ plying knowledge over time

rows.value: (PDF p. 13) Conclusion — The conclusion: everyday uncertainty reframes uncertainty as a situated, ongoing and life-long process, and the field should go beyond precision-focused objectives like accuracy and bias mitigation, address the limits of model-specific design and evaluation, and develop strategies to mitigate uncertainty at its core.
quotes: We present a qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews with 20 blind screen reader users to understand their practices with GenAI tools. We introduce the concept of everyday uncertainty to articulate the core experience of blind people’s use of GenAI tools for access, reframing uncertainty as a situated, ongoing, and life­ long process. Drawing on the concept of everyday uncertainty, we articulate future directions to advance AI research for accessibility. We call to go beyond precision-focused objectives like accuracy and bias mitigation, addressing the limitations of model-specific approaches to design and evaluation of AI, and developing strategies to mitigate uncertainty at its core

rows.value: (PDF p. 12) Evaluate in the real workflow, and over time — Nothing in this study measures what anyone can do with or without these tools. It is an interview study and says so; there is no task, no test, no before and after, and the one behavioural change reported - that Be My AI cut down calls to volunteers - is self-reported. Against the requirement that a capability measure fall after the support ends and outside the arrangement that delivered it, neither half is present. The authors then ask for exactly the missing study: long-term work on how these tools affect users' experiences over time.

For instance, to optimize the search ex­ perience, tools could help users quickly identify named entities in AI responses and link them directly to relevant web search results (e.g., see recent work on interactive LLMs as potential examples [64, 124]). cards.title: TableTalk: Scaffolding Spreadsheet Development with a Language Agent
cards.meta: 2025 · ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction · doi 10.1145/3765286 · Route C

rows.value: other
framework or design space, design principle, primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

The paper is explicitly and operationally grounded in scaffolding and sensemaking-process precedents. It adopts Reiser’s task-structuring account of scaffolding, implements Pirolli and Card’s knowledge-product workflow as a requirements-to-schema-to-insight plan, and uses programming-strategy research to motivate flexibility when expert procedures do not fit local context. TableTalk reifies this lineage through contextual next-step choices, rapid intermediate representations, and composable atomic actions. Mixed-initiative guidance informs its stop/undo implications. The paper evaluates this coupled performance-support configuration during spreadsheet work, but it neither isolates the principles experimentally nor implements fading or measures post-support learning or transfer.

medium · The paper provides explicit lineage, three derived principles, rich formative evidence, and a multi-method controlled evaluation. Confidence is reduced by small samples, two short and deliberately difficult evaluation tasks, bundle-level rather than component-level testing, prototype latency, formula errors, and the absence of fading, longitudinal learning, or transfer measures.

items.heading: Claim 1 · S2CARD-CLM-001
items.lead: The transferable mechanism is not generic chat. TableTalk externalizes a domain workflow into a revisable plan, presents contextual alternatives for human selection, and constrains execution to understandable intermediate schemas and components. This is structured performance support during work; the complete bundle was evaluated, but its components were not independently isolated and no fading or post-support transfer was tested.

rows.value: Effective spreadsheet-programming support should couple scaffolding, flexibility, and incrementality: guide users through an expert-derived creation process, adapt next steps to context, and build the artifact from composable atomic components.

items.heading: Claim 2 · S2CARD-CLM-002
items.lead: Externalized structure is not inherently helpful. A static scaffold can expose a useful solution schema while simultaneously imposing comprehension and adaptation work when it is not contingent on the user’s context. Template fit and explainability therefore condition whether structure reduces or increases human work.

rows.value: Static spreadsheet templates supplied problem structure and produced more polished artifacts, but users found them difficult to understand, expensive to assess, and demanding of heavy adaptation, with reduced task completion in the formative study.

items.heading: Claim 3 · S2CARD-CLM-003
items.lead: The coupled scaffold shifted immediate work away from low-level problem solving and verification toward requirements while producing more preferred artifacts. These are short-horizon artifact and process benefits, not evidence of completed-task productivity or learning: no participant completed either deliberately difficult task, latency remained a cost, and the two-task evaluation limits transfer.

cards.title: Investigating How Generative AI Affects Decision-Making in Participatory Design: Shifting the space to make design choices
cards.meta: 2024 · Nordic Conference on Human-Computer Interaction · doi 10.1145/3679318.3685384 · Route C

rows.value: other
framework or design space, design principle, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

A NordiCHI 2024 analytical paper from a participatory design project with 15 older adults with rheumatic disorders, designing keyboards. A tool transcribes what participants say and turns it into design proposals with SDXL; more than 15,000 were produced. Two analyses follow and neither includes a participant. Seven researchers, the authors among them, judged 100 proposals the same researchers had selected, against five qualities: concept, clarity, context, newness, socio-materiality. Then four of the authors mapped those qualities onto Bratteteig and Wagner's four kinds of choice, creating, selecting, concretizing and seeing/evaluating. The result is a small two-axis device for saying what a generative support does to a design process, and the paper's own filled-in version of it thins from five marks at creating to a single mark at seeing/evaluating, which the authors call a limitation. The transferable claims run both ways. Everyday speech becomes viable design input, so the technical translation step goes and with it the designer's monopoly on materialising an idea. Against that: polished, fast, plentiful output invites design fixation and premature moves, because less time from idea to proposal means less maturation between seeing and moving; the model cannot be asked to change one part of an image, which blocks revising; participants may bend their speech to suit it; and knowing when to make a design move stays with whoever has the technical grasp. The authors state that the absence of participant input is a significant limitation, which makes every claim about participants' agency a projection rather than an observation.

high · The framework, the trade-offs and the failure modes are stated clearly and are borrowable as they stand, and the evidence that any of them occurs is not in this paper. Its claims are about what generative AI does to participants' choices, and no participant took part in either analysis; the authors say so themselves. The first analysis was seven researchers including the authors, judging 100 proposals those same researchers had selected from more than 15,000 after removing the ones they thought unimpactful; the second was four of the authors reading the first. No count, rate or agreement statistic is reported for any of the five assessment categories, no decision was observed and no interval was timed, yet the paper states that it has proven an effect on decision-making. Read this card as a well-argued map of mechanisms and conditions, not as evidence of outcomes.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The borrowable thing here is the question the paper asks. Not did the support help, but which kind of choice did it move, where the kinds are creating, selecting, concretizing and seeing/evaluating. Crossed with five qualities of the generated output, that gives a small grid any review of semantic support could fill in for a different system, and filling it in forces the reviewer to say where in a process the support actually lands. The paper's own grid is the more interesting result, because it thins as it goes: five marks against creating choices, four against selecting, three against concretizing and a single one against seeing and evaluating, with context the only quality that reaches all four rows. A support of this kind front-loads a design process. It multiplies the options and helps sort them, and it does almost nothing for working out what an option would mean in use, which is the step where consequences are found. The authors read that distribution as an artefact of their data coming from an early project phase. It is at least as likely a property of the support itself, since generating a proposal is what the model does and judging one is what it cannot do.

rows.value: Because our primary focus has been on generating design proposals based on data from an early phase of a PD process, we see in the table that our findings primarily address how the use of generative AI affects the creation and selection of choices. We consider this to be a limitation of our study

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) 4.2 Theory workshop, the four types of choice — The four types of choice as the paper reproduces them: creating, selecting, concretizing and seeing/evaluating, with concretizing explicitly about the power to materialise a proposal sitting with designers rather than participants.
quotes: Creating choices involves expanding the design space within which participants work by revealing different alternatives. This entails creating room to envision possible directions and trajectories, where participants’ collective diversity of needs, capabilities, and contexts mutually contribute to keeping the design space open. • Selecting choices involves various strategies to coordinate a shared understanding of which choices to carry forward in the design process. An essential part of selecting is creat- ing a dialogue among participants to negotiate and debate different perspectives to collectively make a design “move”. • Concretizing choices involves the participants materializing their choices through prototypes or design proposals that manifest the shared understanding. Traditionally, technical knowledge and skills often delegate power to materialize proposals to the designers rather than participants, and this point largely focuses on empowering participants to con- tribute to the realization with their own capacity. • Seeing/evaluating choices involves the space for understand- ing and reflecting on the choices made through testing and evaluating relevant implications for use, practice, and con- text. The consequences of the proposals are explored through use scenarios, informing both designers and participants, where vital questions and underlying assumptions can be evaluated, providing room for making more informed design “moves” for the next step

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the paper's central positive claim and the one most worth carrying, because it names precisely what the support removes: the translation step. In the older arrangement a participant describes something, a designer with technical skill turns it into a representation, and the power to decide what the representation looks like travels with that skill. Here the participant's own recorded words are the prompt and the representation comes back with no designer in between, which is why the authors can say that selection and concretisation are no longer in the designer's hands in the same sense. Two things bound it. The first is theirs: the same evaluation found clarity inconsistent and particular words dominant, so what comes back reflects the intention fairly reliably and the need unreliably. The second is that the removal only runs forwards. A participant can produce a proposal from their own words and cannot revise one, because asking for a change means regenerating the whole image. The technical translation step is gone from making a proposal and still in place for changing one, and changing one is where design iteration happens. That asymmetry is the transferable finding, and it is sharper than the paper's own framing of it.

rows.value: The participants can use everyday language to create choices in the sense that they can more easily explain ideas and get design proposals without translation to “technical language”. Selection and concretization of ideas are therefore no longer in the hands of the designer in the same sense

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A failure mode worth carrying because the property that causes it is the property the support is valued for. Fidelity, speed and volume are what make the proposals useful, and each is named here as a hazard. Polish makes a proposal read as finished and invites fewer suggestions for change. Familiarity narrows the idea to what the familiar object already does. And speed removes the interval in which an idea used to mature between being seen and being acted on, which is the sharpest statement of the trade in the paper and the one a review can use directly, because it says what is lost rather than what fails. The weakness is that the same authors then offer speed and volume as what may relieve the hazard, which leaves the claim without a direction, and nothing here timed a decision or measured a fixation. There is also a boundary the paper does not draw: the appendix grid shows a corpus of photorealistic product shots, so the polish is a property of how this pipeline renders, not of generated proposals in general. What transfers is the named mechanism and the trade it describes, not evidence that either occurs.

rows.value: At the same time, we acknowledge that premature concretization of choices when working with high-fidelity design proposals might narrow the participants’ design space. The hazard of design fixa- tions, making premature choices, and unintentional convergence is a challenge when no designer is leading the concretization. With these challenges, we risk missing out on unexplored choices because of high-fidelity design proposals

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The most useful line in the paper for separating what a support supplies from what it still requires. Producing a proposal is delegated; judging when a design question has been looked at enough to be closed is not, and the authors say plainly that generative AI does not on its own equalise the imbalance in decision-making power. The second half has the same shape. The proposals lower the technical understanding needed to see what a design would be like in use, and someone with a technical grasp is still better positioned to see it, because the consequences that escape are ones an image does not show, such as false triggering from room noise or the privacy cost of a microphone. So the support redistributes the competence needed to produce a candidate and leaves the competence needed to judge one roughly where it was. For a review that has to say what a semantic support does to the person as well as to the work, that asymmetry is the finding: capability requirements do not fall uniformly, and the requirement that survives is the one that the fast, plentiful output puts under the most time pressure. The paper cannot show any of this, and it does state it in a form another study could test.

rows.value: Still, knowing when to make a design move requires skill, which is not evident through the presence of the design exemplars alone. While the process can rely more on the design proposals as ex- emplars to drive it, the designers’ knowledge of “when to move” and seeing/evaluating choices remains an area where generative AI does not alone equalize the unbalance in decision-making power

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: A failure mode that belongs in any map of what semantic support does to people, and one this literature names rarely: the person adapts to the support rather than the support to the person. The mechanism is concrete. The output is sensitive to word choice, certain words dominate whatever else is said, and the prompt is the participant's own recorded speech, so a participant who notices the regularity will start speaking for the model. The authors' phrase is an artificial form of communication, and they see that it would undermine the non-intrusive role they want the tool to have, which is the sharp part: non-intrusiveness was the design goal, and this particular intrusion is invisible. The conversation still happens, in the participant's own words, and those words are no longer theirs in the sense that mattered to the project. It is a hypothesis, since nobody in this study spoke to the tool. But it is a hypothesis with a named mechanism and a named cost, which is the form in which an open question earns a place in a review.

rows.value: Misinterpretation or unintended behavior due to issues related to semantics or syntax of everyday non-technical language can also provoke a behavior where partici- pants adjust their natural dialogue to align with the AI’s behavior and desired output [54]. items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: An inversion worth recording. In most accounts a semantic support that misreads its input has failed; here the misreading is counted as part of what the support is for, because a proposal nobody would have made is a choice that would not otherwise exist. The paper's own example is exact: a participant asked for a keyboard that could sit at an angle, and the system returned a musical instrument, which the experts file under context failure and the authors also count under newness. What keeps the position from being a rationalisation is that the paper marks where it stops. Divergence with no contextual grip leaves the space to create choices exactly where it was. Abstraction past a point produces images that cannot be discussed at all. And the same variety that opens the creating step obstructs the selecting step, which has to go from many to fewer. So the usable principle is conditional: unreliability is a resource in the divergent phase and a cost in the convergent one, and the same property of the same system does both within one session. That is the shape a conditional finding should have. It is stated here with no measurement behind it, and by experts who chose which proposals they would judge.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: This belongs on the card as a claim rather than a caveat, because it fixes what the rest of the card can be used for. A participatory design paper about how a tool changes participants' choices was written without asking a participant anything. The authors say so, and give their reasons, and the paper calls itself an analytical investigation, so the absence is not concealed. What the reported detail adds is that the substitute was not an independent panel: seven researchers including the authors judged 100 proposals those same researchers had selected out of more than 15,000, having first removed the ones they judged not impactful enough, and the second analysis was four of the authors reading the first. That is a designer's reflective account of their own system, which is a legitimate and often valuable genre. The mismatch is in the grammar. The paper says it has proven that the AI's inconsistency affects participants' decision-making. For a review assembling what is actually known about semantic support, this is the recurring shape to record: a well-argued account of a mechanism, offered in the language of a result, with the person the mechanism concerns absent from the room.

cards.title: A Meta-Analysis of Tangible Learning Studies from the TEI Conference

rows.value: other
review or meta analysis, framework or design space, failure or counterevidence

A review of every tangible learning paper in fifteen years of the TEI conference, 92 of 720, and a useful specimen for two reasons. It makes scaffold learning one of its three headline findings, elaborated into a table with six dimensions, and the construct arrives with none of its machinery: across all seventeen pages the folded text contains zero occurrences of fading, fade, withdraw, contingency, zone of proximal development and Vygotsky, against ten of scaffold. Here scaffolding means the tool makes the task easier while you hold it. The other reason is the review's audit of its own field, which is unusually honest. Of 92 papers 67 ran a user study, 54 of those ran a single experiment lasting between ten minutes and three hours, most had fewer than 50 participants, 60 datasets were qualitative against 23 quantitative, and the whole claim that tangibles beat other interfaces rests on eight comparative studies with a number of others finding no difference. The authors conclude that effectiveness should be viewed with a rational and critical mind. The paper is titled a meta-analysis and contains no effect size, no moderator, no confidence interval and no pooled estimate anywhere.

medium · Reliable about its corpus, weak about effects, and mislabelled. The sampling frame is exhaustive within one venue, 720 TEI papers screened to 112 then to 92 on two stated criteria with two authors reading each paper, and every included paper is listed in Table 9 with title, year, type and age group, so the corpus is checkable and reusable. What it is not is a meta-analysis: the folded full text returns zero occurrences of effect size, moderator, confidence interval, random effects, heterogeneity and p-value, and two of significant. Findings are counts of papers making a claim, so more than 26 studies found a positive impact is a tally of authors' conclusions, not of measured effects, and the sources are the primary papers' own reporting with no quality appraisal or risk-of-bias step. No inter-coder reliability is reported for the framework coding. The survey adds 14 conveniently sampled participants whose opinions are quoted alongside review findings. Take the descriptive statistics about the corpus, the design-space inventory and the authors' own critical section as sound; take every effectiveness statement as a vote count.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: Scaffolding as a synonym for helping, in a 2022 ACM venue, with the whole construct reduced to the benefits an object confers while you are holding it. The review makes scaffold learning one of three headline findings and expands it into a table with six dimensions: concept understanding, cognition, task performance, tolerance of errors, creativity and self-regulation. Every one is a property of the tool in use. Folding all seventeen pages to lowercase alphanumerics gives ten occurrences of scaffold and zero of fading, fade, withdraw, contingency, zone of proximal development and Vygotsky. Nothing in the review concerns how much support is given, whether it is adjusted to the learner, or what remains when it is gone. This matters beyond the one paper because tangible learning is where the artifact is unambiguously external and removable: the objects can simply be taken off the table, so the withdrawal measurement is cheaper here than almost anywhere, and nobody in fifteen years of one conference reports it. The self-regulation row is the sharpest instance. Its two entries are about exposing the interface's structure so learners can see how it works, which is a claim about transparency, and it is filed under the heading that would elsewhere mean the learner no longer needs the support.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: A field auditing itself, with the numbers printed so the audit can be checked. Of 92 publications 67 ran a user study at all; of those 54 ran a single experiment lasting between ten minutes and three hours, 22 lasted under an hour, 55 had fewer than 50 participants, and 60 of the datasets were qualitative against 23 quantitative. The comparative claim that tangibles beat other interfaces rests on eight studies, and the authors add that a number of studies found no difference. That is a rare thing to print in your own review, and it is the most useful contribution the paper makes. The consequence worth carrying is structural rather than about tangibles: a single short session with the support present cannot separate a durable learning effect from the novelty of the object, which is the confound these same authors name a paragraph later, and it cannot say anything about what survives the support being taken away. The evidence base for an entire class of embodied supports is therefore about how people behave in one supported hour.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The failure catalogue, and its shape generalises past tangibles. The two named mechanisms are both about attention landing on the support instead of the subject: the novelty of the object distracts, and a learner absorbed in manipulating it skips the text or dialogue that carries the content. Making a support engaging is therefore not free, and the more engaging it is the more of the learner's attention it takes from the thing being learned. The design failures are concrete and reusable as warnings: children could not navigate between paper and screen elements, were confused by seeing their own actions mirrored, and could not cope when the same objects meant something literal in one moment and symbolic in the next. An effect established with adults was not optimised for children. And a machine learning interface made the concept less abstract while learners still could not connect the model to any real application, which is a support that succeeded at its stated mechanism and failed at the purpose. What bounds all of this is that none of it is quantified: these are qualitative observations relayed from single papers, and the novelty confound in particular is never measured, which is unsurprising when 54 of the studies ran once.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Two of the three collaboration mechanisms in this corpus work by removing capability rather than adding it. Splitting the resources a task needs across group members means nobody can finish alone; providing exactly one point of interaction means people must wait for each other. The constraint is the mechanism, and the design intent is stated plainly, to prevent one person from taking over. This is a design-space dimension worth carrying well beyond tangibles, because most catalogues of supports describe them as things that make an action easier, and these make an action impossible in order to produce a different one. It also connects to the withdrawal question from an unexpected direction: a support defined by what it withholds is already reasoning about how much capability the person should have, which is the same axis fading moves along, just fixed rather than changing. The counts are small, three studies using shared resources and five using single-touch against sixteen using multi-touch, and the review reports no outcome for the mechanisms separately, so this is a vocabulary contribution rather than evidence that constraining works.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.small: concept or lineage, contradiction, open question
items.lead: A community auditing its own label, and passing straight through a borrowed one. The review devotes a whole discussion section to whether the systems it reviewed really are tangible interfaces, applies four printed criteria from Markova, and concludes that some are not, even though their builders intended them to be. The named failure is that studies emphasised embodied interaction and ignored the metaphor, the requirement that the physical thing stand for the digital thing in some meaningful way, and that fifteen studies described an object's size, shape and function while ignoring what it was made of. The same paper applies no criteria at all to scaffolding, which is one of its three headline findings. The asymmetry is the transferable observation: a research community will police the term it owns and accept without test the term it imported from another field. That gives a synthesis a concrete diagnostic, since the presence of a construct's name in a corpus says nothing until you check whether anyone applied its criteria, and it explains how a word can survive for fifteen years in a venue while the property it names, withdrawal, appears in none of the ninety-two papers.

rows.value: Markova et al. [83] mentioned that there was an issue to clarify whether a system was a TUI or an interface with some tangible aspects. A similar dilemma happened in the review results, where some studies designed interactions with a physical object, but it might be not counted as a tangible interaction... cards.title: Creative Play and the Role of the Teacher through the Cultural-Historical Activity Theory Framework

rows.value: other
framework or design space, primary empirical, concept or theory

An early childhood teacher's involvement in five-year-olds' construction play at a 'toy factory' area, filmed over five weeks and read through cultural-historical activity theory. Fifteen episodes were selected from four hours of video and sorted into van Oers's four rule types - technical, social, strategic, conceptual - from which the authors derive four activity strategies handed to the children (Solve, Reflect, Share, Connect) and a new construct, the Zone of Proximal Creative Development. Three things are worth carrying. The support is gated on invitation rather than on diagnosis: episode after episode opens with a child asking, and the stated rule is that help must be contextualised and welcomed by the children and must support and not in any way inhibit their play. One episode records a handover device the paper does not name - the teacher, having been told how to mix orange, pretends to have forgotten so that a child supplies the recipe. Another records a child shaking her head at a peer's suggestion and doing it her own way, which the authors read as persistence and risk-taking rather than as help refused. Against that, the evaluation is closed: the teacher is the second author, she selected and coded her own filmed practice with the first author at 90 per cent agreement, no creativity measure of any kind is taken, and the article has no limitations section.

high · The descriptive material is trustworthy and the inferential claims are not. What can be relied on: six play episodes reproduced at enough length to see who initiated, who spoke and what was made; a stated two-level coding scheme with definitions for each of the four rule types; a filmed corpus with the sampling described; and a reflective journal excerpt printed verbatim. What cannot: the teacher in the video is the second author, the researcher, the coder and the doctoral candidate whose thesis this serves, which the paper states as a convenience sample and never treats as a threat; the fifteen episodes were chosen by the authors from their own footage as rich in teacher involvement, so the corpus is selected on the independent variable; the 90 per cent agreement is between two people one of whom was in the room; no creativity outcome is measured at any point, so every claim that involvement enhanced creativity is an interpretation of the same episodes that supplied it; there is one class of 17 children and one teacher; and the article carries no limitations section at all. Carry the episodes and the vocabulary, not the conclusion.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The support in this study is gated on invitation rather than on diagnosis, and the paper is consistent about it in a way that makes the position visible. The findings open by saying the teacher became involved on the children's request; the episodes are narrated that way - Amelia invited Evi, Adam asks her to make a hole, Paul lets her know he needs a box - and the stated rule is that help must be welcomed by the children and must support and not in any way inhibit their play. That is a real alternative in the design space and it is cheaper than everything else in this corpus. Contingency is usually indexed to a model of what the learner can already do, which requires a diagnostic; indexing it to whether the learner asked requires nothing and makes over-support structurally hard, since an unrequested intervention is out of bounds by definition. The costs are the mirror image and are not addressed. A child who does not ask receives nothing, and no episode here involves one. No count of invited against uninvited moves is given, no check on whether the rule held, and Episode 3, where the teacher arrives unbidden with a bag of materials, breaks it without comment.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: A handover device the paper records and does not name. Having been taught by a child how to mix orange, and having repeated the recipe aloud once herself, the teacher waits until the paint runs out and then pretends to have forgotten, so a second child has to supply it. This is withdrawal of the supporter's own competence rather than of a material aid, and it is contingent in the way that matters: she does it only after the children have demonstrated they hold the knowledge. It is a sharper version of the familiar tutoring move of asking a question you know the answer to, because what is faked is not general ignorance but the loss of something the group just gave her, which puts the child in the position of the one who knows. Three consequences for a review of supports. Feigned incompetence is a fading mechanism that costs nothing, needs no schedule and no instrument, and is available to any human supporter. It is not available to an automated one on the same terms, since a system that pretends not to know is a system whose user can no longer calibrate what it knows. And the paper's own framework cannot see it: the move is filed under social rules as children sharing knowledge, and the words withdraw, fade and gradual do not appear anywhere in the article.

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Play Episode 6, the teacher pretends to have forgotten — Episode 6 contains a handover device the paper does not name and does not analyse, and it deserves a name. Having been taught by a child how to mix orange, and having said the recipe aloud once herself, the teacher waits until the paint runs out and then pretends she has forgotten, at which a second child supplies it. This is withdrawal of the adult's competence rather than of a material support, staged so that the knowledge has to be produced by someone else, and it is contingent in the only way that matters here: she does it after the children have demonstrated they hold the knowledge. It is the same move as the classic tutoring tactic of asking a question you know the answer to, but sharper, because what is faked is not ignorance of the topic but loss of something the group just gave her. Two things follow. Feigned incompetence is a cheap fading mechanism available to any human supporter and to no current automated one, since a system that pretends not to know is a system its user cannot calibrate. And the paper's own framework cannot see it: the move is filed under social rules as sharing knowledge, and the words withdraw, fade and gradual do not appear in the article.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: Two small vocabularies of adult support, and both have a shape worth noting against the other taxonomies in this corpus. The four rule types are not four kinds of move: two of them are kinds of readiness. Technical rules are having the right material available at the moment it is needed, and strategic rules are systematic observation so as to know when to step in and how to answer a request. That makes waiting part of the taxonomy rather than a hole in it, which is rare - most support typologies in this literature enumerate only things the supporter does. The four activity strategies run the other way round from usual: Solve, Reflect, Share and Connect are named as strategies the children employ in response to the teacher, and the paper describes them as handed to the children, which at least gestures at the handover the underlying theory requires even though nothing tests it. Two limits. Both sets are derived from the same fifteen episodes they are then used to describe, so they are a vocabulary and not a finding. And no frequency is reported for any rule or any strategy, so the reader cannot tell which kind of support was common, which was rare, or whether all four of anything occurred more than once.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Every position in the evaluation loop is occupied by the same person, and the paper records this as a convenience rather than as a problem. The teacher in the footage is the second author, the researcher and the doctoral candidate whose thesis the study serves. She kept the reflective journal that is used as evidence; she planned the structured lessons the findings credit her with; she helped select the fifteen episodes from her own filmed practice, on the criterion that they were rich in teacher involvement; and she is one of the two coders whose ninety per cent agreement is the reliability statistic. Two consequences. The corpus is selected on the independent variable, so episodes where the teacher stayed out, misjudged, or got in the way could not appear even if they existed. And on the two-part test for a learning claim there is nothing to test, because no creativity measure is taken at any point - before, during or after - so the abstract's claim that the involvement enhanced creativity is an interpretation of the same episodes chosen to display it. The article has no limitations section; the word limitation does not occur in it. This is the most complete version of the pattern the corpus keeps finding, where the party providing the support also decides what the support achieved.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: A new construct is coined on the zone of proximal development and drops the part that made the original a developmental idea. Vygotsky's zone is defined by a gap that closes - what a child does with help today they do alone tomorrow - which is why the construct carries an implication that the help ends. The Zone of Proximal Creative Development is defined here as the space that the teacher's and the children's actions together denote. There is no statement of what would count as a child moving through it, no before and after, and no sense in which the teacher's involvement is provisional; the accompanying sentence is that it is imperative for the teacher to have an active role. The vocabulary count makes the shape of the omission exact. Across sixteen pages the paper says Vygotsky eight times and zone of proximal five, of which two are its own coinage, while fading, fade, withdraw, contingent, gradual, independent, transfer and removal appear zero times each, and scaffold occurs once outside the reference list, in the abstract. This is not a criticism of studying permanent support - a teacher's presence in play may be exactly the kind of housekeeping that never needs to be internalised - but the paper does not make that argument either. It borrows the name of a developmental gap without supplying any mechanism for closing one.

rows.value: Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development provides the conceptual framework that sustains teacher's involvement in children's, creative play. We strongly believe that it is imperative for the teacher to have an active role during creative play... The teacher's and the children's actions and activity denote a Zone of Proximal Creative Development (ZPCD) where children act upon during their creative play.

quotes: Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development provides the conceptual framework that sustains teacher’s involvement in children’s, creative play. We strongly believe that it is imperative for the teacher to have an active role during creative play. In order for chil- dren’s play to move from creation to creativity, the teacher either, as a player, or as a sup- porter, ﬁnds ways to enhance their thinking, skills and ﬁnally their products. The ways Evi acted in the diﬀerent situations, explained earlier, show how she mediated between children and culture (Veraksa et al. 2016). Arts as a form of culture, within the frame- work of creative play generated a lot of potentialities for children to develop skills and attitudes necessary for the development of their creativity. The ﬂexibility of ideas, the persistence and ability to take risks, to reﬂect and transform ideas were discerned in chil- dren’s creative play activities. The teacher’s and the children’s actions and activity denote a Zone of Proximal Creative Development (ZPCD) where children act upon during their creative play

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) Teacher role in play, the ZPD warrant and creative drama as a tool — The warrant for adult involvement: from Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, children can learn with the help of others with more knowledge and skills, and the authors' own earlier work argues that creative drama techniques are cultural tools teachers can use in their play involvement to develop children's role and scenario play skills.
quotes: Drawing on Vygotsky’s work, about the Zone of Proximal Development, we acknowledge that children can learn with the help of others who have more knowledge and skills; these being either peers or teachers. In our previous work, we have supported the important role of the adult in pretend play (Loizou, Michaelides & Georgiou, 2019) highlighting on elements such as creative drama techniques as crucial for adult involvement but also for play skills development in children. So, we suggest that the use of creative drama techniques can be important tools that support children in developing their role and scenario play skills. Thus, creative drama techniques are seen as cultural tools employed by teachers in their play involvement and can further enhance children

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Abstract — The paper's own summary: cultural-historical activity theory is used to analyse an early childhood teacher's participation in children's creative play in order to enhance and support creativity, grounded on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development; video, a reflective journal and planning documents describe episodes from a toy factory play area; the teacher is said to take on the role of mediator and to scaffold the children's creative play using cultural tools; and four activity strategies, Solve, Reflect, Share and Connect, are proposed as handed to children, framing their Zone of Proximal Creative Development.
quotes: This article aims to use the cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) framework to analyse the participation of an early childhood teacher in children’s creative play, in order to enhance and support creativity. The study is grounded on Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development, and highlights teacher’s play involvement and the arts as a cultural context for creativity development. Data sources such as video recordings, reﬂective journal and planning documents were used to describe play episodes from a play area titled the ‘Toy factory’. These were analysed by assigning each one to speciﬁc rules (e.g. technical, conceptual) and then creativity elements (e.g. process, product) were noted. Findings highlight that creative play underpinned by the CHAT framework is a cultural activity in which children and teachers (involvement) participate in the processes of creation and creativity (rules) in the context of the arts (degrees of freedom). Moreover, the teacher takes on the role of the mediator and scaﬀolds children’s creative play, using cultural tools while endorsing creativity elements. This study provides ample ground to propose corresponding activity strategies (Solve, Reﬂect, Share and Connect) as unfolded through the teacher’s actions, handed to children, to support and enhance their creative play experiences thus framing their Zone of Proximal Creative Development

rows.value: (PDF p. 13) Conclusion, and the last line before the disclosure statement — The conclusion: the contribution is a definition of creative play, van Oers's rules made meaningful for it, the arts as its cultural context, and the strategies children need to employ; creative play is affirmed as a mode of cultural activity in which the teacher is a cultural mediator and the children are cultural creators.
quotes: In this paper, we have employed the CHAT framework to deﬁne creative play, and uti- lised Van Oers’ rules within the context of creative play, making them meaningful for this type of play; underscoring the Arts as the cultural context in which children are actively involved to enhance their creativity. Therefore, this study is unique in adding to the exist- ing play literature by providing a deﬁnition of creative play, and extending the CHAT perspective on play by focusing on the teacher’s play involvement. This play involvement created the space where the children employed strategies that supported them in the crea- tive process, and thus enhanced their creative play. This leads to the augmentation of creativity work, as it speciﬁcally provides the strategies that children need to employ to enhance their creativity and thus their creative play. Our study provided empirical data that support and extend the CHAT perspective on play; highlighting children’s involvement in creative play as a form of rule-based cultural activity, and describing the teacher’s use of cultural tools to support creative play. This study aﬃrms creative play, as a mode of cultural activity, during which the teacher is a cultural mediator, and the children are cultural creators

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) The worry about over-involvement, stated once — The over-involvement worry, stated once and not returned to: activity theory expects adults to be active members in children's play, so the authors say they need to consider how this involvement takes place most appropriately to support, and not in any way inhibit, children's play actions.
quotes: Adults with the use of cultural tools can productively participate in children’s play activities and enhance their play abilities. ‘The human mind develops through appro- priating cultural tools in interactions with more knowledgeable cultural others’ (van Oers and Duijkers 2013, 512). The CHAT expects adults to be active members in chil- dren’s play; thus, we need to consider how this involvement takes place most appropri- ately to support, and not in any way inhibit, children

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Introduction, play as a cultural activity — The theoretical stance: play is a cultural activity in which children use peers, teachers, tools, materials and imagination to support their play actions, and the activity-theory reading of play as a product of cultural history is what validates adult involvement in it.
quotes: We concur with the sociocultural perspective that views play as an activity, a cultural activity (Elkonin 1972; van Oers 2013; Vygotsky 1978) during which children use resources; peers, teachers, tools, materials and imagination to support their play actions and enhance their learning. The cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) framework interprets play as an activity, a product of cultural history, in which others are involved thus validating adult involvement in play activity

cards.title: A Meta-Analysis of Scaffolding Effects in Online Learning in Higher Education

rows.value: other
review or meta analysis, failure or counterevidence, concept or theory

A meta-analysis of 64 effect sizes from 18 articles on scaffolding in online higher education, reporting a large pooled effect of g = 0.87 and a set of subgroup contrasts. It is the clearest single case in this corpus of the gap the review is about. Page 3 defines scaffolding by three features, one of which is transfer of responsibility, glossed as reducing scaffolding activities and withdrawing support over time. Page 4 says that in principle all scaffolds are gradually removed, and reports two prior findings that ought to have stopped the analysis: students given faded procedural scaffolds did not perform well, and a prior meta-analysis found larger effects with no fading at all. The article opens with a metaphor about letting go of a child's bicycle seat, and names that release as the point. Then the coding scheme arrives with exactly two moderators — what the scaffolding was for, and who provided it — and fading is not among the things counted. It returns on page 14 as a direction for future research. Meanwhile the largest contrasts in the results are not properties of any support: experimental designs beat quasi-experimental ones by more than two to one, and US studies beat non-US studies.

medium · The reporting is complete and checkable: a pooled estimate with confidence interval and z, a heterogeneity statistic, and per-subgroup k, n, g, standard error, interval and Q for every contrast. The base is small and fragile. Sixty-four effect sizes come from 18 articles, so estimates cluster within papers and nothing models that dependence; several subgroups rest on five effect sizes; heterogeneity is 91% and a single pooled number is headlined anyway. One person coded everything with no inter-rater check, multi-purpose studies were collapsed to their most frequent purpose, publication bias is acknowledged and uncorrected, and only 13 of the 18 included articles can be identified from the reference list. The authors also attribute their unusually large effect to their sample holding more experimental designs, conceding that the headline is partly a property of which studies were selected. Carry the subgroup pattern and the coding scheme as evidence about what this literature counts; treat the pooled magnitude as soft.

sections.title: 4 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The clearest single instance in this corpus of a literature defining its object by a property it then declines to measure. The arc runs inside one article. Page 2 opens with a child's bicycle and names letting go of the seat as the point. Page 3 makes transfer of responsibility one of three distinctive features and glosses it, in the authors' own parenthesis, as withdrawing support. Page 3 quotes Lajoie's four design questions, the last of which is when to fade. Page 4 states the principle that all scaffolds are gradually removed. Page 4 then reports two prior findings that ought to have redirected the analysis: students given faded procedural scaffolds did not perform well, and a prior meta-analysis found larger effects with no fading at all. Page 7 presents the coding scheme, which has exactly two moderators — what the support was for, and who gave it — and fading is not among them. Page 14 returns fading to the reader as something researchers need to begin to explore. Eleven pages separate the claim that withdrawal is constitutive from the recommendation that somebody study it. Nothing in the analysis is wrong; the point is what the analysis was built to see.

rows.value: Finally, transfer of responsibility means that scaffolding must encourage learners to take responsibility for or ownership of learning from those who provide scaffolding (i.e., instructors or peers). To satisfy the purpose of scaffolding, learners should eventually be able to perform tasks independently. Thus, transfer of responsibility emphasizes the importance of reducing scaffolding activities (i.e., withdrawing support) over time... In principle, all scaffolds are gradually removed depending on the learners' level of development... Researchers need to begin to explore issues that yield more practical and strategic results for instructors and instructional designers such as the timing of scaffolding, including decisions related to the fading and elimination of that scaffolding altogether.
