rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Definition and the bicycle metaphor — The definition and the metaphor: Wood, Bruner and Ross's process enabling a novice to achieve what is beyond unassisted effort, illustrated by holding a child's bicycle seat, alternating between holding and releasing as balance develops, and finally letting go — a step the author names as fading.
quotes: Wood, Bruner, and Ross (1976) defined scaffolding as a “process that enables a child or novice to solve a problem, carry out a task or achieve a goal which would be beyond his unassisted efforts” (p. 90). The first author’s favorite metaphor for scaffolding is that of teaching a child how to ride a bike. At first, when a learner starts pedalling, an assistant needs to hold onto the bike seat firmly because the child may lose control. Next, while the learner is learning how to balance on the bike, the assistant needs to alternate between holding on to and releasing the bike seat as learning progresses. Finally, once the learner has a sense of balance, the assistant should let go of the bike, a step known as fading. This process is similar to teaching using small steps, called scaffolding

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Lajoie's four design questions — Lajoie's four design questions quoted in full: what to scaffold, when to scaffold, how to scaffold, and when to fade scaffolding.
quotes: Critical questions to ask when designing scaffolding activities as an instructional strategy include “what to scaffold, when to scaffold, how to scaffold and when to fade scaffolding

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) The three distinctive features — The three distinctive features taken from Belland and Pea: contingency, meaning ongoing assessment of ability so support arrives at appropriate times; intersubjectivity; and transfer of responsibility.
quotes: Based on the definition of scaffolding by Wood et al. (1976), the three distinctive features of scaffolding include (a) contingency, (b) intersubjectivity, and (c) transfer of responsibility (Belland, 2017; Pea, 2004). Contingency refers to the need for an ongoing assessment of students’ abilities with specific tasks so the teacher can provide scaffolding activities. It also requires instructors to provide scaffolding activities at appropriate times

quotes: However, dynamic assessment of learning processes and the consequences of faded scaffolding has not been explored sufficiently in the context of online learning; so far, research has indicated mixed effects on learning outcomes (Ge, Law, & Huang, 2012). For example, Wu and Pedersen (2011) found that students who received faded computer-based procedural scaffolds did not perform well in science inquires. Belland, Walker, Olsen, and Leary (2015) reported larger effects of scaffolding with no fading

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The numbers are reported fully enough to be re-read against the paper's own argument, and re-reading them changes what they say. Sort every contrast by the size of the gap it produces. Discipline: 1.905 for communications against .478 for language and literature, a gap of 1.43. Research design: 1.045 experimental against .422 quasi-experimental, a gap of .62. Country: 1.162 US against .641 non-US, a gap of .52. Now the support itself: the widest gap among the four scaffolding purposes is .71, and strategic scaffolding, at .440 with a confidence interval running from -.235 to 1.115 and p = .202, is not distinguishable from nothing. The widest gap among sources is between peers at 1.813 and computers at .764, and the peer estimate rests on five effect sizes. So the strongest signals in this dataset are how a study was run and where it was published, not what support anyone received. Two further facts constrain the headline. Heterogeneity is 91%, which means the pooled g summarises a distribution that is mostly genuine variation. And 64 effect sizes come from 18 articles, so estimates cluster within papers and nothing models that dependence, which narrows every confidence interval here.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A construct works best on the population it was not built for, and the field reports this as encouragement. The quoted sentence comes from the largest meta-analysis in this area; the authors reproduce it because it lends credence to their own finding of a large effect in higher education, and their closing line makes the same point in their own voice — the benefits seem to increase as learners age. Read straight, that is a warning. Scaffolding was defined as what an adult does for a child who cannot yet do the task alone, and its strongest measured effects are on graduate students and adult learners, who are the furthest from that description. Two explanations fit. Either the intervention called scaffolding in studies of adults is a different thing that has inherited the name, or the outcomes measured in adult populations are the ones most easily improved by any well-organised support. Both are consistent with the rest of this card: a coding scheme that records what support was intended to do and who supplied it cannot tell those apart, because the properties that would distinguish them — contingency and withdrawal — are the two features the paper calls definitional and does not code.

Simply put, scaffolded instruction is beneficial, and the benefits seem to increase as learners age.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Read the coding scheme as a statement of what this literature believes distinguishes one support from another, because that is what it is. Two moderators: the purpose the support was designed to serve, and the party that supplied it. Both are properties fixed before a learner arrives. Nothing in the scheme records how much support was given, though the paper states elsewhere that the doses in its own corpus ranged from 80 minutes to 10 weeks — a factor of roughly a hundred, uncoded. Nothing records whether the support changed during use, which is contingency, the feature the paper calls first among three. Nothing records whether it was withdrawn, which is transfer of responsibility, the third. And nothing records whether the support was present when the outcome was measured, so an effect observed with the scaffold switched on and an effect observed after it was gone enter the same pool with the same weight. The collapsing rule compounds this: a study using two kinds of scaffolding is filed under whichever appeared more often, so the moderator that does exist is a single label chosen by one uncredentialed judgement per study. What the analysis can therefore answer is which category of intention is associated with larger reported gains. What it cannot answer is anything about how a support behaves.

primary empirical, measurement or method, failure or counterevidence, design principle

A 2019 TiiS article on text-only AI interviewers that conduct hour-long structured interviews and infer the interviewee's Big 5 traits from their chat. Four real deployments, 1,280 completed interviews, 606 of them actual job applicants. The core comparison is one hiring screen split between two agents identical except in persona: warm, cheerful Kaya and reserved, assertive Albert. The prediction was that warmth would draw disclosure. The opposite happened, and the authors print it: users confided in and listened to the reserved agent more, while rating the warm one significantly more like a friend. Being liked and being trusted with something costly came apart in the same sample. Three things travel beyond the platform. Trust points two ways at once: more perceived trust meant more willingness to share sensitive information and more conscious self-inflation on an impression-management scale. Perceived personality similarity predicts every rating of either agent, up to 38 per cent of variance, and almost none of the behaviour. And the same unchanged agent was called robotic and repetitive and rated lowest on every dimension in the one deployment where the interview was compulsory homework. The measurement design is the reusable part: trust scored as forwarding the agent's judgement of your biggest weakness to a hiring manager while telling it you disagree. The bound is the engine: inferred traits agree with an established test at 0.294 at best, and a hiring manager shortlisted real applicants from them.

medium · The central comparison is unusually strong for this literature: two agents differing only in persona, split across the two halves of one real applicant pool of 316 in a genuine hiring screen, with two independent behavioural indices moving the same way and a failed prediction reported rather than buried. Four things bound the card. That comparison has one site, because clients chose the agent and almost none chose the reserved one. The compulsion finding, which is the sharpest context result, is observational with no test between deployments and is offered by the authors as a conjecture. The behavioural indices are bespoke to this study with no reliability figure or external criterion. And the trait engine that supplies the individual-difference predictors agrees with an established instrument at 0.294 at best, with 22 of 35 traits below 0.1, which weakens every finding that rests on inferred traits while leaving the two-agent comparison untouched. The authors state most of these limits themselves, including that objectivity and overtrust are unstudied.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is a failed prediction that the authors print, which is what makes it worth carrying. Two agents differing only in portrait, inquiring strategy, influence operators, small talk and wording were run on the two halves of one applicant pool, 157 against 159, in a real hiring screen. The warm agent was rated significantly more like a friend. The reserved agent was the one people confided in, listened to, and trusted at a trend level. Being liked as a friend and being trusted with something costly come apart in the same sample, and the design move that was supposed to buy disclosure, warmth and rapport, bought the wrong thing. The transferable reading is that the conditions under which a person exposes something risky are not the conditions under which they enjoy an interaction, and a support tool tuned for the second may lose the first. Two bounds. The effects are modest, at p under .02 and .04 on index variables the authors constructed. And only one deployment ran both agents, because in every other deployment the client chose Kaya, so the comparison has one site.

This result showed that users are more willing to listen to Albert, an agent with a reserved, assertive personality.

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Section 1, Introduction — Why the personality question is open: prior work says a computer should hold one strong consistent personality, but a warm persona should build rapport while a serious one should command cooperation, and nobody has tested this in a real high-stakes setting.
quotes: Since studies show that interviewers’ personalities directly affect interview outcomes [45, 106], one of our tasks is to equip an AI interviewer with the “personality” of an effective interviewer. This is non-trivial for three reasons. First, existing research suggests that computers should take on one strong, consistent personality [78]. However, it is unclear which personality an AI interviewer should assume in order to achieve multiple interview goals. For example, a warm and cheerful personality may aid in building rapport with human respondents who can then relax and act authentically [9, 59]. On the other hand, a more serious and assertive personality may elicit more respect and better cooperation from the respondents [45, 77]. Second, existing systems stress the use of both verbal and non-verbal cues to express an agent’s personality [54, 87, 77]. However, it is unclear how an AI interviewer can effectively exhibit its personality through text-only expressions. Third, unlike most AI agents, which are used in a laboratory setting, ours will be used in the real world, including high-stakes situations, such as job interviews. It is unknown how an agent’s personality would affect users in such a context.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: Trust points two ways in the same dataset and the paper reports both without setting them against each other. On the impression-management scale, more perceived trust meant more conscious self-inflation: the users who trusted the agent most were the ones most managing how they looked to it. On the sharing index, more perceived trust meant more willingness to hand over information they were uncomfortable with. Both are trust and they pull the interview in opposite directions. The two measures explain why: the IM scale scores what a person claims about themselves on a questionnaire, while the sharing index scores a costly act taken with the agent's own analysis of them. So a trusted interviewing agent gets more risky disclosures and a more managed self-portrait at the same time. For a review of computational support this is a warning about a construct that gets treated as monolithic and good: building trust in a system whose purpose is authentic information can degrade exactly the thing the system is for, and the direction of that trade depends on which behaviour you happen to be measuring. The authors themselves read the impression-management result as people applying ordinary social rules to a machine, wanting to impress those they trust.

quotes: The IM scale [73], also known as a “lie” or social desirability scale, is designed to detect how users consciously favor themselves to impress others. A user rates oneself using a 7-point Likert scale on each of 20 statements, such as “I have never driven over a speed limit.” If a user rates oneself on the scale of 6 or 7 on this statement to indicate that s/he has never driven over speed limit, it is most likely that s/he consciously inflates oneself since the statement describes an extreme situation. In this case, s/he receives one point. After going through twenty statements, a user receives an accumulated total score. The higher the score, the more inflation there is, and thus, the less willing one is to confide in another with honest ratings [73].

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The same agent, running the same five-part script with the same student-age population, was described differently and rated lower when the interview was compulsory. Robotic is the second most frequent free-text descriptor in the required deployment, at 24 of 193 users, and appears in neither opt-in list; repetitive appears there and nowhere else. On the ratings, the required deployment holds the lowest cell in every row that has a comparable Kaya column: enjoyable 2.5 against 3.2 and 3.8, interesting 2.8 against 3.5 and 3.97, trust 3.5 against 3.8 and 4.0. Nothing in the agent changed. For a review of computational support this is the sort of contingency that is easy to lose: whether the person chose the interaction is doing more to their perception of the system than the system's own design is, and a study that reports one satisfaction figure per tool has averaged over it. The evidence is observational, the deployments differ in task and questions as well as in compulsion, and no test compares them, so this is a strong signal rather than a demonstration. The authors raise it as a wondering and do not pursue it.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Perceived personality similarity is the only variable that predicts every perception outcome for both agents, and for the warm agent's quality rating it alone accounts for 38 per cent of the variance, more than the designed personality, the interview context, gender or culture do anywhere in the paper. But it stops at perception. On the behaviour side it predicts willingness to listen weakly, in a model explaining three per cent, and not at all for the reserved agent; and the paper says outright that it cannot confirm the personality-matching literature. So the similarity effect is about how the agent is rated, not about what the user will do. Two things follow. For anyone designing an assistive agent, matching a user's personality buys liking rather than compliance, and liking is what most agent studies measure. And the measure has a problem the paper does not address: perceived similarity is self-reported in the same post-interview questionnaire as the outcomes, so a general halo would produce this pattern too. The paper then uses the correlation between reported similarity and machine-inferred extroversion as evidence that the inference engine is valid, which closes a loop rather than opening one.

rows.value: On modeling users' perceived agent quality, for both Kaya and Albert, we found that only Similar Personality was a significant factor. In other words, users who felt having a personality similar to an agent rated the agent higher on its quality. However, since Similar Personality was not significant, users may not necessarily be willing to listen to an agent who possesses a similar personality. We thus are unable to confirm previous findings.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The traits that drive every finding on this card, and that a hiring manager used to shortlist real applicants, agree with an established personality instrument at a maximum of 0.294, under nine per cent of shared variance, and 22 of the 35 traits fall below 0.1. Reliability reaches the conventional threshold for 19 of 35 traits and only once a person has produced about a thousand words. The authors report all of this plainly and say more validation is needed, which is to their credit and is also the point: an instrument at this level of agreement is being used to rank people. Two further gaps sit beside it. Objectivity is offered as a reason for building the agent in the introduction and conceded as never measured in the future-work section; the training data is a million sampled Twitter users plus known-group exemplars picked by profession, which is a specific population rather than an absence of one. And the authors state they have not studied whether a user might overtrust the agent or what that would cost, while citing work showing people do overtrust machine-inferred traits. For a review of computational support this is the case where the measurement instrument, the deployment decision and the unexamined risk are all in the same paper and the paper names two of the three.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: The measurement design is the part of this paper most reusable outside it. Trust in an agent is scored not as a Likert rating but as a costly act, and weighted by how much the person disagreed with what they were being asked to share: the index rises highest when a user forwards the agent's assessment of her biggest weakness to a hiring manager while telling the agent she thinks it is wrong. The listening index works the same way, adapting the classic Desert Survival persuasion paradigm so that the agent's suggestion competes with the user's own answer for a slot that a third party will see. Both indices put something real at stake for the participant, which is unusual and is what lets the study distinguish liking from trusting. That distinction is the card's other findings: perceived similarity predicts the ratings and not the acts, warmth predicts being called a friend and not being confided in. The price is that the indices are bespoke, defined only by two worked examples and a formula, with no reliability figure and no validation against any external criterion, so cross-study comparison is not available.

rows.value: As seen from the example actions above, we designed user actions to measure one's willingness to confide at multiple scales instead of as a binary value (sharing vs. no sharing). Moreover, we design the actions to measure the sensitivity of the information to be shared. The less confidence a user has in the information, the more sensitive the information is. By our measure, a user is most willing to confide in an agent if she shares the most sensitive information with a third party.

rows.value: (PDF p. 19) Section 6.2, sharing actions — The graded sharing action: the agent shows its inferred top weakness, the user rates it, and a user counts as most willing to confide if she shares the agent's version even while disagreeing with it.
quotes: Table 3(a) provides two example actions used in our field deployments. The first one is to share a user’s biggest weakness. The agent asks a user about her biggest weakness before showing its inferred top weakness for the user. The agent then asks the user to rate the inferred weakness by a 3-point rating (Table 3(a)). Heuristically, this rating measures the “sensitivity” of the information to be shared. If a user disagrees with the system-suggested weakness, this weakness information might be more sensitive and a user might feel more risky to share such a weakness with someone who has influences. As part of the action, the user must choose one of three actions (sAction in Table 3(a)). The user’s rating and choice of action are then used to compute the user’s willingness to confide in an agent (A in Table 3(a)). By this measure, a user is most willing to confide in the agent if she shares her weakness suggested by the agent, even if she disagrees with its analysis.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: This is the paper's practical justification and it is the claim most likely to be cited loosely, so it is worth writing down exactly what it is. A hiring manager shortlisted 60 candidates from trait rankings instead of from resumes; 16 of them were later rated Excellent against 6 in a comparable prior round, and screening time fell from a couple of weeks to about two hours. There is no control. The two rounds involve different applicant pools in different years, and the ratings were made by the same manager who knew which process had produced the shortlist. The authors concede they could not build a competence model from the sample. What is more defensible is the throughput and reach: 316 hour-long interviews completed in three weeks, a shortlist described as drawn from more universities, and the manager's own statement that some of the 12 he picked in the other deployment would have gone unnoticed from resumes alone. For a review, this is the shape of the efficiency evidence that gets carried forward in this literature: real, useful, uncontrolled, and one step short of an outcome measure that would settle whether the assessment was any good.

cards.title: Language Migration in non-CS Introductory Programming through Mutual Language Translation Environment

rows.value: other
primary empirical, framework or design space, design principle

About a hundred art students at a Japanese university take an introductory Java course in an environment that translates both ways between a Scratch-style block language and Java, and after four weeks of compulsory exposure to both they are simply allowed to choose, assignment by assignment, which one to work in. The tool logs the seconds. Block use falls from a mean of 0.6 of working time near the start to 0.4 in the middle to 0.1 at the end; the bottom 10% of students never touched the block editor at all, the top 10% were still using it in the final week, and the other 80% moved across on wildly different schedules. Students who rated their own skill lowest used blocks most — 0.44 and 0.41 for the two lower self-ratings against 0.25 for the highest, significant against the lowest group at p < .05 on n = 11 versus n = 28. This is one of the few designs in the corpus where withdrawal is neither on a timer nor decided by a diagnosis but chosen by the learner, and the trajectory is actually recorded. What is not recorded is any measure of programming ability: there were no paper tests, the outcome is the tool's own usage log, and the authors say so — 'we analyzed only the language selection rate. This is not direct evidence that the learners' understanding is being enhanced.' Their own figure also shows the drop is a cliff at the one long assignment where programs passed 400 lines and blocks became unmanageable, not the smooth decline the text describes.

medium · The behavioural trace is real and unusually complete: about 100 students, fifteen weeks, per-assignment working time logged automatically with idle gaps over five minutes excluded, and a per-student grid that shows the spread rather than only the mean. Carry that. Everything else is weak. The only outcome variable is which editor the student had open, which is the tool's own log; there is no test, no code measure and no post-course assessment, and the authors say so. The one comparison to the previous year's all-Java cohort is a recollection with no data, instrument or statistic, offered beside an unmeasured claim that classroom atmosphere improved. The self-evaluation analysis rests on a single four-point self-rating, with the high group at n = 11, Welch degrees of freedom near 13, and one of two comparisons only marginal. And the paper's own Figure 3 contradicts the word gradual: use rises for a month, then falls off a cliff at the assignment where programs reached 400 lines, which the authors attribute to blocks becoming hard to manage. Treat the migration curve as evidence about tool choice under a scaling limit, not about learning.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A third regime of withdrawal, and the corpus has very few examples of it. Fading here is neither on a timer nor triggered by a diagnosis: after four weeks in which both languages were compulsory, every remaining assignment simply let the student pick, and the support was left behind by whoever decided to leave it. Two things transfer. First, the design makes withdrawal observable without asking anyone: because the environment logs working time per editor per task, the trajectory is a measurement rather than a design intention, which is more than most fading claims in this literature can show. Second, what it shows is that a single schedule would have been wrong for almost everybody. Ten percent of students never used the support at all and ten percent had not left it by the final week, with the other eighty percent crossing at visibly different points, and many of them working in both languages at once on the same task rather than switching cleanly. A fixed fade date set anywhere would have taken the support from people still using it or removed something a fifth of the class had already abandoned. That is the strongest argument this paper makes, and it is an argument about design rather than about learning.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: Optional support usually routes itself away from the people who need it most, because weak learners are weak help seekers and often do not realise they need help. Here it did not: the students who rated their own skill lowest spent 44% of their working time in the block editor against 25% for the students who rated themselves highest, and the gap between the extremes clears p < .05. That is a positive result about a voluntary support and worth recording as a counterexample, with three cautions attached. The independent variable is a single four-point self-rating, not a measured skill, so what this shows is that self-perceived weakness predicts help taking, not that actual weakness does — and the paper cannot distinguish a student who correctly judged themselves weak from one who was merely diffident. The high group is eleven people, and both Welch tests run on about thirteen degrees of freedom, with one of the two comparisons only marginal. And the two lower groups, 47 and 28 people, are almost identical at 0.41 and 0.44, so the finding is really that the small self-confident group used blocks less, not that use tracks self-rating along a scale.

rows.value: The descriptive statistics were as follows: G (n = 11, sd = 0.25, avg = 0.25), NG (n = 47, sd = 0.20, avg = 0.41), NGA (n = 28, sd = 0.15, avg = 0.44). Welch's t-test was conducted between groups G and NG and between groups G and NGA. The difference between G and NG was marginally significant (t(13.29) = 2.04, .05 < p < .10). The difference between G and NGA was significant (t(13.15) = 2.39, p < .05). These results show that students who evaluated their programming skills as low selected to use BlockEditor more often than did students who rated their skills as high.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The paper concludes that a block language successfully acts as scaffolding for learning text-based programming, and the only thing it measured is how long each student had which editor open. Put that against the two-part test — a learning measure has to come after the treatment ends and from outside the arrangement that delivered it — and it fails both halves, because there is no measure at all: the course had no paper tests by design, no code was scored, and no assessment followed the course. What stands in for one is the tool's own log, which is the sharpest version of a pattern this corpus keeps meeting, where the evidence for a support is produced by the support. Here the log has an additional peculiarity: the quantity taken as evidence of success is the support's own disuse, so the better the number looks, the less the instrument was running. What the authors offer against their stated limitation is a recollection of the previous year's cohort with no instrument, no numbers and no test, hedged inside 'in the range of our observations', plus a report that the classroom atmosphere changed from negative to positive and a statement of strong belief. Those are the three families of evidence in the wrong proportion: the encounter and the process are recorded in detail, and the person afterwards is not recorded at all.

The negative atmosphere in the classroom was dramatically changed into a positive one. We strongly believe that the results will encourage teachers who use a block language in introductory programming education.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The authors supply their own best counter-argument and do not follow it up. Their Figure 3 does not show a gradual decline: block use climbs for the first month, reaching about 0.8, then falls almost vertically at the single assignment where students had to build their own game and average program length hit 400 lines, after which it never rises above about 0.15 again. The stated reason is that the block editor became difficult to manage at that size. So the curve everyone would read as learners outgrowing their scaffold is at least as consistent with a scaling limit in the tool: the support did not become unnecessary, it became unusable, at a moment chosen by the assignment schedule rather than by any student. This is a general hazard for any withdrawal claim resting on declining use of an optional support — the task got harder and the support did not scale is a rival explanation for the same curve, and only a capability measure can separate them, which is the measure this paper does not have. Two smaller design facts point the same way. The round trip collapses every Java loop form into one repeat block, so a program taken back into blocks loses the distinction the learner is meant to be acquiring; and the editor shows no blocks at all for Java that does not parse, so the support vanishes exactly when the learner is stuck.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: This is the precondition of learner-elected withdrawal, named out loud, and then granted. If the learner decides when to stop using the support, the diagnosis that a contingent system would have to perform has been moved inside the learner, and the whole design now rests on that judgement being sound. The authors see this clearly enough to raise it, and then supply three warrants, none of which is a measurement: that the students are at university, that they were shown both languages first, and that many used blocks only partially without being taught to, which is read as awareness of their own understanding. That last step is circular — varied behaviour is offered as evidence of accurate self-assessment, when varied behaviour is exactly what would also be produced by taste, habit or convenience. It matters because the corpus has the opposite finding on record, that weak learners are weak help seekers because they often do not realise they need help, and because this paper's own self-rating data show a group of eleven students who thought they were good and used the support least, with nothing to say whether they were right. The general point to carry: a system that fades on a fixed schedule needs a schedule it cannot justify, and a system that lets the learner fade needs a self-assessment nobody checks. Both of them are the same missing diagnosis in different hands.

cards.title: Human Performance Consequences of Stages and Levels of Automation

rows.value: other
review or meta analysis, design principle, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method, concept or theory

The paper that turned the automation trade-off from a saying into a number. Eighteen experiments, pooled by ranking each study's effects as significant or not and averaging Kendall's tau. As the degree of automation rises, performance while it works improves (tau +.51 over 16 studies) and performance after it breaks down, when the operator must take the task back, gets worse (tau -.34 over 9 studies); eight of the nine studies measuring both show the routine correlation as the more positive one. The authors call it the lumberjack effect: the higher they are, the farther they fall. Two things make it valuable to a review of semantic support. It defines and takes the withdrawal measure directly — performance on the task after the support is gone — and it concludes there is no safe setting, no degree below which the benefit can be raised for free, which kills the field's standing advice to pick a medium level. In its place it puts a stage rule: keep the person in choosing the action, because choosing is what preserves the ability to act. Three cautions, all readable off its own Table 1. Only 9 of the 18 studies measured withdrawal at all. The celebrated critical-boundary result, -.90 on withdrawal, has data from two of the six studies it names. And the workload benefit the Key Points assert fails the paper's own one-tailed test at p = .056, the single unstarred cell in the table.

medium · The central trade-off is as well established as this literature allows and the within-study pairing makes it hard to explain away, so direction and existence are secure. Everything else is bounded by the same three facts. The synthesis carries no effect sizes at all, by necessity, so no magnitude is estimated anywhere. The counts thin out fast below the headline: nine studies for the withdrawal cost, eleven for the awareness mechanism with two running the other way, and two for the withdrawal half of the critical-boundary result the abstract calls most interesting. And one advertised half of the trade-off, the workload benefit, fails the paper's own one-tailed test at p = .056 while the Key Points state it as fact. The authors name most of these limits themselves, which is why the card can be this specific.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is the quantitative statement of the thing a review of semantic support most needs and most rarely gets. More support makes the supported work go better and makes the person worse at the work once the support is gone, and the two move together: tau +.51 for routine performance across sixteen studies, tau -.34 for performance after breakdown across nine, and in eight of the nine studies that measured both the routine correlation was the more positive of the pair. That within-study pairing is the strongest part of the evidence, because it is not vulnerable to different studies being different. What makes the claim carry beyond automation is that nothing in it depends on the support being machinery: it is a claim about what happens to a capability that is exercised less. The asymmetry in the evidence base is itself the finding for us. Sixteen studies measured the benefit and nine measured the cost, so the field that owns this result still measured withdrawal only half the time it measured help.

rows.value: We found (a) a clear automation benefit for routine system performance with increasing DOA, (b) a similar but weaker pattern for workload when automation functioned properly, and (c) a negative impact of higher DOA on failure system performance and SA. Taken together, results for primary task performance support the hypothesized lumberjack effect as the routine and failure aspects of performance trade-off with increasing automation complexity.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The single most reusable idea in the paper, and the thinnest evidence in it. The claim is that the cost of support is not spread evenly along a scale of how much help you get: it is concentrated at one place, where the support stops telling you about the situation and starts choosing what to do. Support that analyses and leaves the choice with you is cheap; support that makes the choice is expensive. The mechanism offered for it is the generation effect: having chosen the action yourself is what keeps you able to act. That is a mechanism about meaning-making, not about machinery, and it transfers directly to any support that produces a candidate answer rather than material to reason from. But the number attached to it will not bear weight. Six studies are named. Table 1 records return-to-manual data for two of them, Manzey and Reichenbach, whose values are -.816 and -1; their mean is -.908, which is the -.90 the text reports. The finding the abstract calls most interesting has a withdrawal half computed from two experiments.

rows.value: Most interesting was the finding that negative consequences of automation seem to be most likely when DOA moved across a critical boundary, which was identified between automation supporting information analysis and automation supporting action selection. Actively choosing actions manually (the generation effect; Slamecka & Graf, 1978) supports SA in a way that supports the manual performance in case of automation breakdown. When that choice is removed, the automation failure response suffers.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The design conclusion, and it is a negative one worth carrying. The field's standing advice, from Endsley and Kiris, was that a middle setting buys most of the benefit while avoiding most of the cost. This analysis says there is no such setting: because the two curves trade off directly, every increment of support that helps also costs, and the search for a safe level is a search for something the data do not contain. What replaces it is a different kind of rule. Not how much support, but which part of the work it takes: keep the person in choosing and doing, and the cost stays low even at high support elsewhere. That converts a quantity question into a structural one, which is the more useful form for anyone designing a support rather than tuning a dial. It also quietly refutes the paper's own opening figure, which draws the cost as flat up to a high degree and marks a recommended operating point on that flat stretch. The results found no flat stretch.

rows.value: Each step of increase of DOA seems to be associated with an increase of the risk of return-to-manual performance decrements, meaning that there is no specific DOA below which automation-induced performance benefits can be increased without any performance costs. This renders doubts in any simple design recipes like medium DOAs are best. If return-to-manual performance issues are of serious concern, human operators should be kept involved at least to some extent in decision and action selection as well as action implementation.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The causal story the whole field repeats has its middle link unestablished, and this paper is honest about it. The story is that support takes you out of the loop, awareness of the situation decays, and that is why you cannot recover when the support stops. Here the awareness measure correlates with the degree of automation at tau -.29 across eleven studies, with five showing the loss, four showing nothing, and two running the other way — more automation with better awareness. No mediation is tested anywhere. The support offered for the link is that two studies with the largest routine-to-withdrawal gap also had large negative awareness correlations, which is a coincidence of two rows in a table of eighteen. The post hoc attempt to find a display moderator, which would have been indirect evidence for the same pathway, produced nothing. For a review of semantic support this is the useful shape of the gap: the outcome is measured and the mechanism is not, so a design that aims to preserve awareness in order to preserve recovery is aiming at an untested link.

rows.value: We hypothesized that one of the costs concerned with higher degrees of automation would be associated with LSA. The data presented in Table 1 further suggest that this effect is linked to raised issues of LSA with increasing DOA. However, due to a lack of statistical power, this latter conclusion needs to be treated with caution.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: What this synthesis can and cannot deliver is set by what the primary literature reported, and the authors say so. Effect magnitudes were rarely published, so effects were coded as significant or not, turned into ranks, and summarised as Kendall's tau. Reading the table confirms that each overall tau is the plain unweighted mean of the per-study taus in its column: the sixteen routine values average .5099 and the nine withdrawal values average -.3373, matching the printed .509 and -.337. So a two-condition study and a four-condition study count equally, sample sizes appear nowhere, and no heterogeneity statistic is possible. The consequence is precise and should travel with any citation of this paper: it establishes that the trade-off exists and its direction, and it does not estimate how large the cost is, which is the number anyone deciding whether to accept the trade actually needs. The deeper point for a review is that the ceiling was set by reporting practice in the source literature, not by the reviewers.

rows.value: Departing from the classic meta-analysis approach we assigned rankings for every metavariable within a single study according to significant effects found with regard to DOA. This was done as effect sizes (e.g., Hedges's g) were only rarely reported in the original studies and therefore could not be used for analysis, without eliminating many studies from consideration. A second limitation is the possibility that we might have underestimated the trends within any particular study, with the relatively coarse dichotomous grain size by which effects were coded.

items.lead: A clean, documented case of two inheritances being fused into one measurable quantity by stipulation. Sheridan and Verplank's 1978 continuum of levels — how much autonomy the machine has — and the four-stage decomposition of information processing from Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens — which part of thinking the machine does — are independent axes. This paper declares three postulates that let both count as more automation, and thereby creates a single ordinal degree of automation over which correlations can be computed. The authors are unusually candid about the seam: Case 4, where a later stage meets a lower level, cannot be ranked at all, and they say they have no confidence it ever can be. The construct is therefore defined only over the comparisons the literature happened to run, and they note that none of their studies contained the unrankable case. What makes this worth carrying is the irony at the end: having merged the two dimensions to get a scale, the paper's most interesting result is that the damage lives at a stage boundary and not at a level, which is an argument for keeping them apart.

rows.value: Considering that more automation can be represented both by higher levels within a stage, and, typically, later stages, we assume that these two dimensions increase the degree of automation. All other factors held equivalent, (a) a higher level of automation constitutes more automation, (b) a later stage of automation constitutes more automation, and (c) as a consequence, a combination of higher levels and a greater number of stages at which automation is implemented constitutes more automation. Case 4 is an important exception. It is impossible to assess a relative DOA unless both stages and levels are expressed on an interval or ratio scale, and we have no confidence that this has or even can be done.

cards.title: Ask Systems: Interrogative Access to Multiple Ways of Thinking

rows.value: other
framework or design space, design principle, concept or theory

A design article for a class of support called an Ask System: an interface where the learner picks a question from a fixed set and the system answers, usually with a story told by an experienced practitioner. The paradigm dates from Schank's group around 1991 and the paper surveys a range of built examples, from a radiation-technician curriculum organised entirely around such questions to a teaching help system for engineering faculty, and proposes that the question set be structured differently depending on what kind of thinking is wanted: frequently asked questions, problem solving, metacognitive monitoring, causal reasoning, or multiple perspectives. Two things make it worth carrying. It proposes the measure this review keeps finding absent, saying that transfer should be assessed by the quality of the questions students subsequently ask on new problems, and marks the hypothesis as empirically untested. And it states, of a paradigm that had then been built and deployed for twenty years, that its effectiveness has not been tested empirically in any systematic way. Phrases like another untested use, another potential application and no research has tested that assumption recur throughout. It is an argument for a design, offered by its main advocate, with no evidence of its own.

low · The paper reports no study, and says so about the whole paradigm it describes: the effectiveness of Ask Systems has not been tested empirically in any systematic way, twenty years after the first ones were built. Individual sections are candid in the same way, calling uses untested and assumptions unexamined. What the article offers is a design vocabulary, a set of worked examples of built systems, and a research agenda. Two further cautions. The examples were selected by the author, several from his own projects, and are described rather than evaluated. And the one substantial empirical result imported to support the paradigm, a question-prompt study, is reported without the limitation its own authors attached to it, which matters because that limitation is precisely that the prompts and the outcome measure addressed the same processes. Carry the design vocabulary, the proposed transfer measure and the author's own statement of the evidential vacuum; carry nothing here as an effect.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The measure this review keeps finding absent, proposed in print and not taken. The proposal is unusually practical: to find out what a support left behind, watch what the person does on a new problem when the support is not there, and specifically watch the questions they ask unprompted. That requires removing nothing and building nothing, only looking at the right thing afterwards, and it has a validated basis since question quality is a strong predictor of comprehension and problem solving. The hypothesis it would test is also the one this design most needs, because the interaction is built so the learner never formulates a question: they are written in advance by experts and the learner selects from a list. Whether choosing among someone else's questions teaches anyone to compose their own is exactly the point at issue, and the author says plainly that it is untested. What makes this worth carrying is that the withdrawal question is not being overlooked here; it is stated correctly, given a workable operationalisation, and left as future work.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: A class of support invented around 1991, built repeatedly, deployed in corporate and military settings and in a full technical curriculum, and by 2011 never evaluated for effectiveness. The statement comes from the paradigm's principal advocate, in an article arguing for it, which is what makes it usable evidence rather than a polemical claim: the person with every reason to cite a positive result reports that there is none. The candour runs through the paper, which introduces its examples as designed and developed although unfortunately not researched, calls one variant another untested use, and notes of a central design assumption that no research has tested it. What supports the paradigm instead is named honestly too: theoretical rationale, observation of use, and the argument that building one forces a designer to think about the learning required. For this review the transferable point is about how design paradigms propagate. Deployment, elaboration and advocacy all accumulated for two decades without the evaluation, and nothing in the process required it, which is the same pattern found elsewhere in this corpus where a requirement is cited faithfully and never built.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The article's real contribution is a design-space dimension: for a support built out of questions, what the questions are about is the design decision, and it can be chosen to match the kind of thinking wanted. That transfers directly to any prompt-shaped support, which is most of the supports in this corpus: a checklist, a review template, a set of reflection prompts and a code-review rubric all make the same choice, usually without noticing it. The worked example from the radiation curriculum shows what it costs to do properly, since the question set came out of months of negotiation with experienced practitioners and is meant to reproduce what they actually reflect on. What is missing is any evidence that the match matters. The author says as much about the closely related assumption that the type of information returned should suit the question structure, noting that no research has tested it.

Two properties are lost in the substitution and the paper does not mark either. A practitioner reflecting while working responds to this situation; the system holds answers written in advance for situations anticipated by whoever was interviewed, so it cannot notice that the case in front of the learner is unlike the ones it knows. items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The paradigm's strongest imported evidence, and a small demonstration of how qualifications get lost. The study cited is real and its result is reported accurately: students given prompts tied to four problem-solving processes produced better reports on all four. What does not travel is the warning its own authors attached, that the prompts and the scoring rubric addressed the same four processes, so the advantage may have been on the assessment rather than on the problem. That caveat is in the discussion section of the paper being cited, and the authors also name the transfer study that would resolve it. Here the finding arrives without it and supports a conclusion about helping students monitor and regulate their problem solving. Nothing dishonest is happening; this is ordinary citation practice. It matters for a review because it means the second-hand literature systematically reads stronger than the primary literature, and any synthesis that works from citations will inherit an optimism the original authors did not have. It is also worth noting what the citation does establish: that prompts of this shape change what people produce while they have them, which is not in dispute.

cards.title: Context-aware prompting to transition autonomously through vocational tasks for individuals with cognitive impairments

rows.value: other
design principle, primary empirical, failure or counterevidence

An assistive technology paper that hands this review a vocabulary it needs and then shows what happens when the vocabulary is implemented without its mechanism. The doctrine it inherits is the system of least prompts: a job coach begins with the least intrusive cue, waits, and escalates through gesture, model and physical guidance only while the trainee keeps having difficulty. That is diagnosis, graded contingency and withdrawal in one named practice, and it is expensive because a person must run it. What the authors build instead binds prompts to places: a Bluetooth beacon at each work station, attenuated to a radius under two metres so the cue lands before the person walks past, firing a picture and a voice prompt indexed by the intersection of this beacon and this particular worker. Timing is solved by making the world carry it. Nothing escalates, because a beacon cannot tell whether the step succeeded. Eight adults with cognitive impairments filled a nine-step coffee-shop order three ways and the device won, six at full correctness against a spoken baseline ranging from zero to ninety per cent. The result reported against the authors own interest is that a printed paper note put six of eight above eighty per cent, which they say made them realise why the note remains job coaching most popular method. Two participants scored at ceiling with the device and did not want it, one because his employer would see him using it and one because he preferred a person beside him; a third understood the picture prompts and could not use them while her hands were in the work. Autonomy is the stated goal and it means stimulus control moving from a human to a machine, the opposite of fading: nothing is measured with the device taken away, and asking for help was scored as an error.

high · Treat every number here as a demonstration rather than a result: eight people, one trial per condition, each condition on its own task set in a fixed order, and no statistics. The card's durable content is elsewhere — a named practice of graded contingent prompting that the system does not implement, a definition of autonomy under which the support never leaves, and three individual reports that separate a support working from a person wanting it.

cards.title: The learner centric ecology of resources: A framework for using technology to scaffold learning

rows.value: other
framework or design space, concept or theory, design principle, primary empirical

A framework paper, written up from a keynote, proposing the Ecology of Resources as a way to describe a learner's whole context so that technology can be designed to marshal it. Its content is six slots in three pairs around one learner: the Knowledge and Skills to be learnt, filtered by a Curriculum; the Resources that might help, people and artifacts alike, filtered by an Administration; and the Environment, filtered by its Organisation. Each pair sits in a shaded area standing for the history it carries. The theory is Vygotsky's zone of proximal development pushed outward through two constructs of the author's own: the Zone of Available Assistance, everything a context happens to contain, and the Zone of Proximal Adjustment, the subset that suits this learner now. The point is that resources are not assistance until someone selects and activates a subset. Relationships carry as much weight as elements: two-way links tie the three elements to each other and the three filters to each other, but the arrows from Knowledge and Environment to the learner are one-way, because a learner rarely changes what counts as valid knowledge or the timetable. A designer chooses whose ecology this is, fills the six slots, draws the links, and looks for missing links and tensions inside a slot. Two applications are shown. HOMEWORK, a tablet system linking home and school maths for five to seven year olds, was designed and evaluated first and mapped onto the framework afterwards, its reported gains summarised with the detail referred out. VeSEL, an agricultural project in Kenya, is walked through slot by slot but was mid-prototype with no outcomes. The framework itself is never evaluated, and its most operational moment is a pair of diagrams of designs that were never built.

medium · The framework's content is firm: the six slots, the three pairings, the arrow rules and the two zones are stated unambiguously in the text and drawn in Figures 1 and 2, and the Kambu fill shows what applying it looks like. Everything about its value is untested. It is never evaluated against any alternative; the one system with outcomes was designed and evaluated first and mapped onto the model afterwards, so the analysis describes a success rather than having produced one; those outcomes are reported without a single number, with the detail referred out; the two counterfactual designs that make the framework look operational were never built; and the second application had no results at all. The author is candid, naming the labour-intensity confound herself and saying usefulness in informal settings still requires investigation. Two internal strains are this card's reading, not hers: the one-way learner arrows rest on one observation about tutoring software and are contradicted by the paper's own closing argument, and the reciprocal-expertise point removes the more able partner the ZPA needs. The page text is clean throughout, so no quote came from a substitute page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is the framework, and it is small enough to state exactly. One learner at the centre; three things that learner may reach, Knowledge and Skills, Resources, Environment; and three filters that stand between the learner and each of them, Curriculum, Administration, Organisation. Resources explicitly include people as well as technology and artifacts, so a parent, a teacher and a wind-up radio occupy the same slot. Two further provisions widen it: the centre may hold a group rather than an individual, and teachers and parents deserve ecologies of their own; and every element, plus the learner, arrives with a history that places it in a wider cultural and political system, drawn as shading around each pair. The pairing rule is what makes the framework useful rather than a list of context factors. It says a designer's problem is rarely that a resource is absent and usually that a filter governs access to it, and it names the filter as a separate object to be inspected. The author notes that the filters vary in strength, a curriculum being tighter for maths than for plumbing, which is a scope note that matters when the model is carried outside formal schooling. What the framework does not supply is any criterion for when an ecology is adequate, or any weighting among elements.

rows.value: The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources Model of Context attempts to pull together this previous work and the theoretical underpinnings of the ZPD, ZAA and ZPA as we consider a learning context as an Ecology of Resources: a set of inter-related resource elements, including people and objects, the interactions between which provide a particular context. The learner is the starting point for our Ecology. In an educational situation there will also be some 'stuff', Skills or Knowledge that our learner needs to learn about and some resources that might help this learner learn that 'stuff'. However, the 'stuff' to be learnt is usually filtered through some kind of organisation or Curriculum and has been subject to a process of validation. Likewise the resources that may be available to the learner are organised in some way. We use the word Administration to convey that here. We need to add Environment to our model in Fig. 1. In doing so we also need to recognize that in the same way that a learner's access to Knowledge and Resources is mediated by Curriculum and Administration so too a learners access to the Environment is mediated by its Organisation.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The most transportable idea in the paper, and the one that carries a design consequence beyond this framework. Availability is not assistance. A context can be thick with people and tools and still produce no learning, because a zone of proximal development requires that someone select and activate the subset that fits this learner at this moment. The two zones give that a vocabulary: everything the setting contains, and the part of it that is currently right. The author offers two ways to do the selection and they are different jobs. Making existing help visible to the learner is an interface problem; representing the learner's needs so that she and the people around her can choose is a modelling problem. The paper does not say when to prefer which, nor what makes a selection correct beyond the inherited contingency rule from Wood, take over control on an error and hand it back on success, advising one level above the learner's current success. The construct also carries the paper's clearest lineage claim: scaffolding is treated as one way the zone of proximal development and its timely interventions have been used in teaching, from Wood, Bruner and Ross in 1976, and the Ecology of Resources is presented as the same idea pushed out of the software and into the world.

rows.value: The ZAA is used to describe the types of resources, both human and artifact, that are available within a particular context to help a more able partner to offer appropriate assistance to a less able learner. The ZPA represents a selected subset of the ZAA that are the resources that are the most appropriate form of assistance for a given learner at a particular moment in time. The existence of a rich set of resources within the ZAA is not sufficient to ensure the interactions necessary to create a ZPD for the learner. As well as being a resource themselves, the more able partner is also responsible for ensuring that the resources available within a particular environment are organized and activated appropriately for that learner to form a ZPA. This may simply mean making obvious to the learner the forms of assistance that already exist within her environment or finding a way to represent the learners' needs so that she and the other stakeholders in the process of her learning can select appropriately.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The relationships are what this paper adds to its own earlier descriptions, and the arrow directions are the only part of the framework that could be wrong in an interesting way. Three claims are packed in. Elements influence each other, so what is to be learnt, what could help and where the learning happens are mutually constraining; the paper's example is that formal subject matter is taught where the resources are of a particular kind. Filters likewise influence each other, so curriculum, administration and organisation move together. And the learner's own influence is asymmetric: she can change the resources and their administration, because her activity alters adaptive software and the software alters her, but she cannot change what counts as valid subject knowledge or, usually, the timetables and regulations that organise her environment. The evidence for the asymmetry is one observation drawn from tutoring systems, generalised to knowledge and environment at large, which is thin for a claim doing this much structural work. It also sits awkwardly with the paper's own conclusion, which argues that cheap capture and publishing tools are extending the making of learning contexts beyond teachers and designers, that is, dissolving the very asymmetry the diagram fixes.

rows.value: Hence in Fig. 2, which illustrates this Ecology of Resources approach there are bi-directional arrows linking Knowledge, Resources and Environment, and linking Curriculum, Administration and Organisation. However, the arrows between a learner and her Environment and between a Learner and the Knowledge she seeks are uni-directional. This software scaffolding activity meant that a learners' interactions with the software were bi-directional, in other words the learner's activity altered the nature of the software and vice versa. The same cannot be said for a learner's interactions with the subject matter being learnt: it was and largely still is unlikely that their activity will make any difference to the nature of what is accepted as valid subject knowledge or skills.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: This is the only place in the paper where the framework does work rather than describe it, and the move is worth stating precisely: draw the ecology a candidate design would create, and read off which links between elements it fails to make. Figures 4a and 4b are the same diagram as Figure 2 with different arcs deleted, and they form a matched pair. A personal laptop with no contextualised content buys the link between resources and environment, because the device travels, and loses the links that tie knowledge to resources and to environment, because nothing relates the maths met at school to the maths met at home. Contextualised content delivered online to a home PC buys the knowledge-to-resources link and loses the reach across environments, because the machine cannot leave the house. Only the built system holds both. Stated this way the framework yields a checkable design question, which pair of elements does this design leave unconnected, and the question carries to artifacts that have nothing to do with tablets. The limits are real, though. Neither alternative was built, so both diagnoses are readings of a diagram rather than observed failures; the only system ever mapped was mapped after it had already succeeded; and the mapping is qualified by the author herself as covering a small part of the curriculum and a limited range of resources and environments.

rows.value: Secondly, it offers us a framework within which we can evaluate existing technology interventions by exploring of the extent to which all the relationships depicted in Fig. 2 are in place. For a small part of the curriculum and a limited range of resources and environments the HOMEWORK system addresses all of the links between the elements in Fig. 2. For example, a system that offered each child their own personal device, a laptop for example, but did not provide the interface that links learning across locations or the specifically contextualised activities and associated scaffolding, could result in a situation such as that illustrated in Fig. 4a. However, without the contextualized activities and integrated interface the technology resource offered to the learner and those who wish to support her may not enable them to relate the knowledge and skills experienced within one location to those experienced in another. Alternatively, if the HOMEWORK interface, activities, personalisation and scaffolding were offered as an on-line system that could be used via a home PC then we risk a situation such as that depicted in Fig. 4b. The result is that the contextualisation between knowledge and environment will be reduced and the potential for technology to link resources across locations is limited.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: This is the paper's only measured strand, and it is reported at summary level by the author's own admission, with detail and analysis referred out to Luckin et al. 2006. What is here is a real and substantial programme: six design phases with over forty teachers from eighteen schools and more than eighty families, then a four-week and a two-week study with more than thirty children, a teacher and parents, using researcher notes, video, logs, diaries, interviews, questionnaires and pre and post learning tests. What is reported from it is thin relative to that scale. Learning gains are asserted with no measure, no numbers and no comparison group. The lesson comparison is described as a small observation study and yields time on task, waiting time, and observed attention and engagement. The mental arithmetic finding is one teacher's impression, and the teacher herself declines to attribute it, saying she does not know whether it came from the tablet or from the child's mother. The author raises the obvious confound, that the gains came from more adult labour rather than from the design, and her answer half addresses it: researchers supported technology rather than taught, but parents genuinely did teach more, which she reclassifies as a benefit rather than controlling for it. That is a defensible position for a design programme and a weak one for an efficacy claim, because any comparison against ordinary homework is then a comparison of two different amounts of adult help. None of this is evidence about the framework, which was applied to the system afterwards.

rows.value: The increasingly functional prototype HOMEWORK system was evaluated at several stages, including a 4-week and a 2-week study, involving home and school use of the penultimate and final functional prototype system by more than 30 children from a rural village primary school, their teacher and parents. The pre-and post test results evidenced learning gains. A small observation study that compared a maths lesson where the HOMEWORK system was used with a maths lesson where the system was not in use revealed that when the HOMEWORK system was used more time was spent on doing maths, with little or no time spent by children waiting for attention. The children also displayed increased attention and engagement in the learning task when using the HOMEWORK system tablet PCs. For the purposes of this discussion it is important to note that the empirical studies demonstrated that when designed and used appropriately educational technology could improve links between home and school learning and close the gap between parents, teachers and learners.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: The empirical part of the paper that is genuinely about work rather than about learning gains, and the part that most directly earns the framework its Organisation slot. School organisation was known; home organisation was not, and turned out to be both variable and consequential, the difference between a car outside a ballet class and a kitchen at teatime being a difference in what a design can assume. Two findings have design force. First, roles are unstable at home: a parent is a supplementary teacher and simultaneously a learner, picking up the curriculum, how to teach maths, and sometimes numeracy itself. Second, and more useful, parental availability did not convert into assistance by itself. Diaries and interviews found parents wanted to help but needed explicit guidance about how, and the activities had to be designed to invite collaboration. That is the ZAA-to-ZPA distinction showing up in the field: the resource was present in the ordinary condition too, and what the design added was activation. Teachers' conditions were equally concrete, that they would customise if the technology fitted normal practice and institutional constraints, and that they wanted to see where each child had got to. The author's closing note, that introducing technology can change roles and organisational constraints, is stated flatly and without evidence beyond these cases.

rows.value: The UK school organisational context was a relatively 'known quantity'. However, the home organisational context is relatively unknown and far more variable. For example, the organisational context for a learner who is in the car waiting for his sister's ballet lesson to finish is very different to the context where a learner is sitting at home while her mum is making tea. In addition to this, the roles are less stable in the home context. Parents might be conceived of as supplementary teachers but they also become learners in this context. Parents wanted to help their children, however they needed to be given clear guidance about how to help with homework activities and these activities needed to be designed to encourage parental collaboration. It should also be noted that the appropriate introduction of technology can undoubtedly change roles and organisational constraints.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: The Kambu walkthrough is the paper's only prospective use of the framework and the best evidence that the six slots generalise beyond schooling. It is also where the vocabulary strains productively. There is no curriculum, so the Curriculum slot takes two organising forces at once, an agricultural expert's validated guidance and the community's traditional beliefs carried as stories, and the framework's contribution is to place them in the same slot where their conflict becomes visible as a design problem rather than a background fact. Administration behaves the same way, absorbing both a named person who keeps the resource kit and unwritten customs and practices that govern who may ask whom for help. Naming an informal norm as a filter, and putting it where a designer must look at it, is the most useful thing the framework does here. The Environment slot then does concrete work: little electricity, no internet, children without desks, long distances, which is why a bicycle that carries and powers the kit is the right resource and would not have been in England. And the procedure is stated as a procedure: identify the elements present, use that to indicate where interventions might be made, map candidate interventions on to see how they support the essential links, identify tensions, and use participatory design to inform how the tensions are tackled. What it does not do is resolve anything. The framework produces a list of what must be decided; the deciding is handed to participatory design and the wider cultural context.

rows.value: The Skills or Knowledge that our learner needs to learn about are those that relate to water management with respect to growing water melons in arid conditions. This agricultural knowledge is not part of a formal curriculum. However, the aim is to instill good practice and the information that will be provided by the VeSEL resources will be organised according to the guidance validated by our agricultural expert. There will also be accepted community beliefs about good farming methods, that will be organized according to tradition, as stories for example. If we consider each of the elements in our Ecology factors that impact on the design process for our educational technologies can be identified. For example, if we consider the Curriculum filter that organizes the knowledge to be learnt it is clear that there is a potential tension at this point in our Ecology between what the community believes to be good farming practice and what current agricultural expertise believes to be good practice.

items.heading: Claim 8 · CLAIM-008
items.lead: The paper's closing move, and the place where it turns its own framework against itself. If learners marshal resources to build an ecology that meets goals they set, the one-way arrows from Knowledge and Environment to the learner become two-way, and the more able partner is no longer the person who selects the zone of proximal adjustment. The author sees both consequences and states them. The second is sharper than it looks: contingent teaching and the ZPA both require a partner who can judge the learner's current level and pick the right help, but if the adult knows the subject and the child knows the tool, no single party can make that judgement. The paper names this as an opportunity for reciprocal teaching and learning, says the more able partner should be both teacher and learner with respect to different expertise, and admits English lacks a word for the relationship, reaching for Bruner's learning by transaction and the Russian obuchenie. It then says plainly that we do not know how to scaffold learners to generate their own contexts and that new educational theories will be needed for situations where the balance of control keeps shifting. This is an honestly declared gap rather than a result. The definition offered is broad enough to cover most goal-directed collaboration, so as it stands the construct marks a direction of travel rather than a category a designer can use.

rows.value: What we might call a Learner Generated Context can be defined as a context created by people interacting together with a common, self-defined goal. For example, if we accept the view that a context can be described as a user centric Ecology of Resources then a Learner Generated Context is one in which a learner or group of learners marshall the resources available to them to create an ecology that meets their needs. The key aspect of Learner Generated Contexts is that they are created through the enterprise of those who would previously have been consumers in a context created for them. However, in order to progress this agenda we need to increase our understanding of how to scaffold learners to effectively generate their own learning contexts. We now face a situation in which the teachers and experts, who know more than the learners about the 'stuff' we want people to learn, may well not know as much as the learners about the technologies that could act as learning tools.

There is now a real opportunity for reciprocal teaching and learning.
