cards.title: An Online Support System to Scaffold Real-World Problem Solving

rows.value: S2W-90BCF6F3F9D8A8B92D613C79
other
primary empirical, framework or design space, design principle

A 2005 description of a web system for teaching ill-structured problem solving, built from five parts: a case library, question prompts an instructor can author at two levels of detail, an expert's worked response, peer review, and reflection prompts. Two studies are reported. The first is a proper randomised comparison of prompts against no prompts with 63 students, and the prompted group roughly doubled its problem-solving score and beat the control on every sub-process measured. The second varied how much scaffolding students got and its performance analysis was unfinished at publication, so only interviews are reported. Three things in those interviews are worth more than the headline. Detailed sub-prompts produced more thorough reasoning than top-level outline prompts, so granularity behaves like a dose. Students who could not see peer feedback did not know what to revise and left their answers essentially unchanged, which makes the revision step inert without a peer signal. And students said the reflection prompts made them reflect deliberately in a way they would not have done unprompted. The system requires an answer before it will show the expert's, a principle the authors argue for explicitly against a contemporary system that did not.

medium · Study 1 is a genuine randomised comparison with 63 participants, a real no-prompt control, and results reported per sub-process rather than as a single composite, which is stronger evidence than most of this corpus offers. Everything after that is weaker. Study 2's quantitative comparison is explicitly unfinished at publication, so the granularity, peer feedback and reflection findings rest on interviews with no counts, no coding procedure and no analysis of the online transcripts the authors say corroborate them. Both studies come from the authors' own group and Study 1 is reported second-hand from their own prior paper. The system is described as adaptive throughout, but adaptivity here means instructors can author prompts for new domains and database tables can be reused, not that anything responds to a learner; the authors name learner adaptivity as future work.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A randomised comparison against a genuine no-prompt control, with the outcome broken out by sub-process rather than reported as one composite. That breakout is what makes it useful: prompts moved problem representation, solution development and argument construction separately, so the overall effect is not a single strong component carrying two flat ones. The magnitudes are large, roughly double, which for a single-session intervention on graduate students should invite some caution about what the outcome measure rewards, since a scoring rubric built around the phases the prompts name will credit students who wrote about those phases. The companion result is more interesting for this review: self-rated competence rose in the prompted group and not in the control, so confidence and measured performance moved together here, which is the opposite of the pattern in the AI code-generation studies where confidence rose alone.

rows.value: The results showed that novice learners who had received question prompts not only scored significantly higher in overall problem solving performance than those who did not receive question prompts, but also significantly surpassed their peers in the control condition in each of the problem solving processes, i.e., problem representation, developing solutions, and constructing argument.

The same phases of problem solving were named in both conditions; only the depth differed, top-level headings against headings with sub-questions underneath, and the difference showed up in how thoroughly students could explain their own approach. items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: Removing the peer signal did not make revision worse; it made revision not happen. Both conditions had the same reflection step and the same expert response, and the condition without peer feedback left its answers essentially untouched, because the students could not tell what needed changing. cards.title: Expertise in design: an overview

rows.value: S2CW-E3522328F6F774A08EBEEB92
other
review or meta analysis, concept or theory, lineage or history, failure or counterevidence

A review of protocol and interview studies of design expertise, arguing that designers do not behave the way expertise research from well-defined domains predicts. Experts are solution-focused: they propose early and use the proposal to find out what the problem is, and problem and solution co-evolve toward a matching pair, which the paper shows has been named four times over as problem setting, problem paradigm, primary generator and co-evolution. Two findings cut against what is taught. Experts fixate on their first concept and patch it rather than replace it, and the review argues that educating this away may destroy something that works, while noting that both too few and too many alternatives were found equally weak. And time spent defining the problem helps seniors and harms freshmen, with one group of students for whom gathering data had become a substitute for designing. On externalisation the review carries the strongest claim available: unexpected discoveries in a designer's own sketches drive the invention of new requirements, and inventing requirements produces further discoveries. It closes by warning against importing models of expertise from other fields and by naming its own method's blind spot, that protocol analysis cannot see non-verbal thought.

medium · Read this as the field's account of itself in 2004 rather than as evidence about any system. Its definitional claims are the most settled part and are what the corpus needs. Its empirical claims arrive at one remove from small protocol studies, several of them on students, and its interpretation of fixation as a productive feature rather than a limitation is contested inside the paper. The author names the method's blind spot and closes by saying the issues remain open.

It also names the resource being drawn on: framing is possible because of prior experience of this problem type, which is exactly what a newcomer lacks and what a support would have to stand in for.

cards.title: Designing Desert Houses in the Knowledge Integration Environment.

rows.value: other
design principle, primary empirical, concept or theory, failure or counterevidence

A short AERA panel paper about a middle school thermodynamics unit in which students design a house for the desert inside the Knowledge Integration Environment. Its argument is that open knowledge-building systems got students generating questions and hypotheses but not developing constraints or building coherent arguments, and that a design problem supplies the missing convergence, because success in design is the fit between criteria and solution and nothing can be settled by proof. Justification and the coordinating of multiple perspectives is what the authors take knowledge integration to be. The sharpest line for this review is a diagnosis of their own field: the trouble getting students to contribute was wrongly blamed on empty environments, and procedural guidance, templates, libraries and even reflective prompts were not enough without substantial help from teachers. What the software puts in front of a student is a small annotated library of evidence filed by part of the house, a discussion seeded with two named design strategies, and a heat flow worksheet whose arrows cannot be drawn without committing to a direction and a rate justified by a principle. None of it responds to what this student did; the library's categories were built from what earlier cohorts produced, and the only responsive support is a person. Nothing fades. Knowledge integration is defined and never scored: the assessment section is future tense, the one reported result is an unquantified increase against previous semesters, and the measurement is deferred to a companion paper.

medium · Take the design descriptions at face value and treat every effect claim as an observation. The authors built and ran this activity over several semesters and describe what they built precisely; they report three outcomes without a single number between them, compare against previous semesters, and defer their one measurement to another paper. The most valuable claims here, that a rich static support was not enough without a person and that worked examples narrowed the design space, are also the two with the thinnest warrant: the first carries no citation at all and the second no count.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The move worth carrying is that the authors do not add a support to the environment, they change what the task rewards. Their claim is that argument only appears where nothing else can settle the matter, so if you want justification you have to build a problem that cannot be closed by a right answer. That is a design lever this review sees rarely, since most of the corpus adds a prompt or a panel to a task whose success criteria stay untouched. The definition attached to it is unusually clean: knowledge integration is the justifying and the holding together of several perspectives, not a store of facts. Its weakness is that the whole thing is an argument. The divergent and convergent contrast is borrowed from one cited page, the design problem definition is Goel's, and the hypothesis in the abstract is never put at risk anywhere in the eight pages.

rows.value: Students in intentional learning environments such as CSILE could generate the divergent side of knowledge building, questions and hypotheses, but had difficulty with the convergent processes of developing constraints and formulating coherent arguments. Properly scaffolded design problems supply what was missing, because a design problem's success is measured by the fit between the design criteria and the solution, and because a design cannot be settled by a proof or a single piece of evidence but only by argumentation, negotiation and the application of criteria. It is this process of justification, of coordinating multiple perspectives, that contributes to and in some sense defines knowledge integration.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the most useful paragraph in the paper for S2Q3 and it is also the least defended. The list of things that were not enough, procedural guidance, templates, libraries and reflective prompts, is close to an inventory of what this review studies, and the authors report that all of it together did not get students contributing without a person present. Two things follow. First, the corrective reflex the field reached for, adding content to a thin environment, is named here as a misdiagnosis, which is worth having in a corpus where the usual remedy for a support that underperforms is to make it richer. Second, the term they use for what was missing, context-sensitive guidance, is the same distinction other papers in this wave draw between a support planned in advance and a person who reads the situation. Against that, the whole passage carries no citation, no count and no case, and it is written by people invested in the successor system. Treat it as a well-placed hypothesis about failure, not as a finding.

rows.value: Difficulty getting students to contribute productively to student-generated community knowledge bases and other open-ended computational mediums was incorrectly assigned to the lack of initial content in these environments. Use of procedural guidance, templates and libraries, even reflective prompts, was not enough in many cases to scaffold students so that they could contribute productively without substantial help from teachers or armies of graduate students. Teachers had difficulty with these projects because of interrelated factors including difficulty structuring problems, students' lack of ownership of the work, and a lack of context-sensitive guidance; simply providing forums for the exchange of ideas and resources is not enough.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The best-told failure in the paper and one this review can use directly. A support meant to teach a concept taught a shape instead: students were shown mud, straw and brick to make them think about insulation, and they built mud domes. The general form is that anything concrete a support puts in front of someone is a candidate answer as well as an illustration, and people take the answer. The authors locate the damage precisely, at the moment the problem definition should be widening, which is more useful than the usual warning about fixation. Two details make it stronger. Making the example schematic was only a partial fix, so abstraction reduces the pull rather than removing it. And the thing that finally worked was social, a rule that you had to reconcile your design with someone else's, which means the effect came from the activity structure rather than from anything on the screen. What is missing is arithmetic. Many, more principled and wider are the only quantities given, and the comparison is with earlier semesters of the same course.

rows.value: The initial examples which students see constrain their process of design at the very point when we want to encourage a broader problem definition. In the pilot study, a comparison of a mud, a straw and a brick house intended to focus students on the insulating value of materials produced, not surprisingly, many dome-shaped mud houses. Later iterations used more schematic examples in an attempt to provide conceptual rather than concrete models. Finally, requiring students to merge their design with their partner's led to more principled evaluation of alternatives and a wider range of original designs, which balances the development of constraints against the need for an expanded problem definition.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Worth recording because this is one of the canonical scaffolded inquiry systems and the answer is unambiguous once you look for it: nothing in the software reacts to the individual student. The library returns the same results to the same query for everyone, the discussion is seeded with the same two positions for the whole class, and the worksheet is one sheet. The only contingent supports in the activity are people, and the paper says so plainly when it lists the two routes to the relevant factors. The interesting part is where the adaptation went instead. It went backwards in time and sideways to the group: the categories a student meets were derived from what earlier cohorts produced, so the system learns from students in general between semesters rather than from this student during the task. That is a real design position and a defensible one, and it should be named as such rather than read as a limitation of 1998 technology. The caution is that the authors never draw this line themselves, so the claim is mine assembled from their description.

The discussion tool is seeded in advance with comments reflecting two design strategies, and the same strategies are mirrored in the library. Students can identify the relevant factors by independently examining pieces of evidence or through interaction with their teacher and peers, and what KIE contributes is social support in the form of collaborative tools and discussion spaces.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: This is the part of the paper that is squarely about designed structure carrying task-relevant meaning, and the design is better than the evidence for it. Three structures are made to coincide: the categories of the collection, the parts of the thing being designed, and the sections of the document to be written. Once they line up, finding evidence and drafting the report become the same act of filing, and the decomposition of the task is legible in the shape of the library rather than stated in an instruction. The library also carries its own provenance, the query that found each site and the design strategy the evidence supports, which is a form of showing the work that most modern retrieval interfaces have dropped. Two cautions. The alignment is only affordable because the collection was curated small and the task decomposition is fixed and known in advance, which is exactly what open-ended professional work does not offer. And the claim that a bounded collection prepares people for an unbounded one is the paper's only statement about what happens once the support is gone, and it has nothing behind it.

rows.value: The library contains examples of different components of the house along with annotations describing how the site relates to the heating and cooling issues of the house design problem. From a guidance perspective, the Design Library models the process of searching for and critiquing evidence by providing the queries used to locate the site, annotations of the scientific material, and links to design strategies supported by the evidence. Since these resources relate to specific components of the problem, it is easier for students to link pieces of evidence to sections in their final design report, and the categories for the design library map onto the components found in student designs, which helps make the process of decomposing the task visible for students.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: The mechanism is the interesting part and the measurement is close to absent. Rather than issuing a rubric, the design plants two rival positions in the class's own discussion and repeats them in the library, so a student meets the criteria as things people disagree about instead of as a checklist. The authors give a reason for preferring that: criteria come into being while evidence is being assembled behind competing solutions, so a criterion handed over in advance is a different object from one a student arrives at. This is a genuine design principle and it generalises past school science. The outcome offered for it is one clause with no arithmetic in it, comparing an unspecified number of students against unspecified earlier semesters, with no account of how a student's strategy was classified. There is also an unexamined risk: the same paper shows examples narrowing the space they were meant to open, and two seeded strategies could as easily become the only two strategies. The authors do not consider that, and they end the section saying making criteria visible is still the challenge.

rows.value: Peer review and collaboration are most productive when students have common metrics for critiquing each other's work, and evaluating design problems is difficult without shared criteria given the range of possible solutions. Developing shared criteria is challenging because it requires students to articulate implicit methods of evaluation, and our research suggests that students need help structuring open-ended problems if they are to develop explicit criteria. To help students identify different positions and solution paths, we seeded the SpeakEasy discussion with comments reflecting two distinct design strategies, insulate versus store and release heat energy, and mirrored those strategies in the Design Library. The result was an increase in the number of students using the more complex heat capacity strategy as compared with previous semesters.

cards.title: Designing Computer Learning Environments for Engineering and Computer Science: The Scaffolded Knowledge Integration Framework.

rows.value: S2W-641CD5F78A90BF7DE8BCA93B
other
framework or design space, concept or theory, primary empirical

The paper that named Scaffolded Knowledge Integration, and it matters here for what it kept and what it changed. Transfer of responsibility survives from the original definition and is called a major component — but it is reinterpreted. It no longer means a support diminishing over time; it means renegotiating who has authority in the classroom, so that students evaluate evidence instead of asking the teacher what is right. Nothing in this framework diminishes. The word fading does not appear, nor withdrawal, nor contingency, and Vygotsky is cited once for the idea that social support helps. The framework is also unusually honest about its own hazards: making thinking visible, its second principle, is said to risk teaching students to memorise rather than integrate, and its fourth principle, social support, is reported backfiring on the women in both courses. And the evidence for it is an equity result — in the programming course the gender gap in grades closed to zero across four semesters, and the help fell hardest on the students who arrived with least.

low · A framework paper illustrated by two course-refinement programmes, and it makes no claim to be anything else: the method is trial, refinement and synthesis across successive versions of a course, with no control group, no random assignment and no comparison against an alternative design. The quantitative evidence is two tables of course outcomes by gender across four semesters of one programming course and one pre-post in one engineering course, with effect sizes but no inferential test on the trend, and everything confounded with time, instructor learning and cohort. The four framework aspects are a synthesis of prior work rather than a tested structure, and the author says so. Two things make it worth carrying anyway: it is the source document for a framework this corpus meets again downstream, so its wording is evidence about the lineage rather than about learning, and its self-reported hazards are unusually candid for a paper advocating its own framework.

sections.title: 4 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is where transfer of responsibility goes when scaffolding moves from tutoring into environment design. It survives — the framework calls it a major component — but its content changes. In the 1976 account responsibility passes because the tutor does less of the task as the learner does more; here it passes because the classroom's authority structure is renegotiated, so a student evaluates evidence instead of asking the teacher what is right. Those are different operations. The first is temporal and forces a decision about when to stop; the second is epistemic and can be arranged in week one and left in place all term. Nothing in this framework diminishes, and the words fading, withdrawal, contingency and temporary do not appear in twenty-four pages. Read this way the framework does not drop the third feature of scaffolding so much as reinterpret it into a form that needs no withdrawal — which resolves a puzzle downstream, because the 1998 implementation study of the same framework describes a student-facing environment where nothing is ever taken away, and in doing so it is not deviating from this document, it is following it. The paired caution is the fading dilemma in its non-temporal form and is stated better here than in most of the corpus: hand over responsibility without the skill to exercise it and the learner flounders, as in guided discovery.

rows.value: A major component of the scaffolded knowledge integration framework is transferring responsibility for understanding to the student. This means renegotiating the authority structure in most classrooms such that students learn to evaluate evidence rather than relying on the teacher to say what is right. Yet at the same time, if students are given responsibility without skills necessary to exercise that authority, they may flounder rather than integrate their ideas, as was often observed in guided discovery learning programs... Thus, encouraging autonomous learning involves both transferring responsibility and ensuring that students can exercise the responsibility effectively.

quotes: Scaffolded knowledge integration is a method for encouraging students to develop integrated un- derstanding of a complex domain. To achieve inte- grated understanding students link and connect ideas. Students with integrated understanding have a cohesive view of a domain and can apply their ideas to personally relevant problems. Integrated understanding is reflected in students' willingness to look at anomalies and exceptions and try to deter- mine how to fit them into their conceptual frame- work. In contrast, sometimes instruction discourages students from analyzing their own understanding and instead suggests that students just adopt the views presented by the instructor. In science, where intuitive ideas held by stu- dents are often quite different from those of experts, building on student ideas is particularly important (Carey, 1985; diSessa, 1988; Eylon and Linn, 1995; McCloskey et aL, 1980; West et aL, 1984). The scaf- folded knowledge integration framework looks at student ideas as building blocks rather than impedi- ments to understanding (lJnrl and Songer, 1991). items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: Two of the framework's four principles are reported misfiring, by their own author, in the paper that proposes them. Making thinking visible — the second principle, and the one the whole tradition is best known for — is said to risk teaching students to memorise the visible thinking rather than do their own. Providing social support — the fourth — delivered peer criticism grounded in the belief that engineering is a male domain, aimed at exactly the students the equity results say the redesign helped. Neither is a small caveat. They are failure modes of the mechanism rather than of the implementation: an explicit model of expert reasoning is a thing that can be copied instead of understood, and a support that works by exposing a novice to a community inherits whatever that community does to novices. The second is the sharper of the two for this review, because it identifies a support whose harm falls specifically on the population the intervention was for, and because it is the one aspect of the framework the author leaves open — this aspect requires further investigation. Papers proposing frameworks do not usually publish their own failure modes, and both belong in the corpus's catalogue of ways support backfires: not by not working, but by working as designed on a mechanism that has a second edge.

quotes: Scaffolded knowledge integration is a method for encouraging students to develop integrated un- derstanding of a complex domain. To achieve inte- grated understanding students link and connect ideas. Students with integrated understanding have a cohesive view of a domain and can apply their ideas to personally relevant problems. Integrated understanding is reflected in students' willingness to look at anomalies and exceptions and try to deter- mine how to fit them into their conceptual frame- work. In contrast, sometimes instruction discourages students from analyzing their own understanding and instead suggests that students just adopt the views presented by the instructor. In science, where intuitive ideas held by stu- dents are often quite different from those of experts, building on student ideas is particularly important (Carey, 1985; diSessa, 1988; Eylon and Linn, 1995; McCloskey et aL, 1980; West et aL, 1984). The scaf- folded knowledge integration framework looks at student ideas as building blocks rather than impedi- ments to understanding (lJnrl and Songer, 1991). As a result, students are encouraged to reconcile anomalies rather than just memorize isolated pieces of information

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Two things worth carrying from the framework's opening move. First, its third criterion for choosing what to teach is to provide students with the resources to continue the sense-making process after they finish the current course. That is the after-support condition, written into a design framework in 1995, and it is doing real work — the heat-flow model is chosen over molecular kinetic theory precisely because students will still be able to use it on everyday problems. It is also the thing the framework never measures. What gets measured is grades and persistence inside the course, semester by semester. The gap between a stated after-course criterion and an entirely within-course instrument is the gap this review keeps finding thirty years later, and here it is visible at the origin of the tradition. Second, the framework defines itself explicitly against the cognitive-tutor tradition: a repertoire of models to be expanded and distinguished, set against instruction that diagnoses a weakness and corrects it. That opposition is worth holding because this corpus contains both branches and they behave differently under removal. The correcting branch produces the sharpest measurable gains and the sharpest losses when correction stops. This branch never tests removal, because on its own account there is nothing to remove — what the student leaves with is a wider repertoire and a different relation to authority, both already theirs. Neither branch has evidence that its gains outlast the course; they differ in whether they think the question applies.

cards.title: Text Organization: Curricular and Instructional Implications for Diverse Learners. Technical Report No. 18.

rows.value: other
framework or design space, design principle, concept or theory

A 1995 University of Oregon technical report that takes an existing research synthesis on text structure and reading comprehension and re-sorts its teaching techniques into six curriculum-design principles, one of which is mediated scaffolding. It is worth carrying for three things. First, scaffolding is defined here as external support supplied by four different carriers — teacher and peers, content, tasks, and materials — and each carrier gets a different ending: teacher and peer support is faded as students gain fluency, content and task scaffolding is not withdrawn at all but is a difficulty ladder, and material scaffolding is kept until students can apply the knowledge independently, a competence criterion with no test attached. Second, withdrawal runs in both directions and is triggered by what the student does: as students gain proficiency the teacher provides less guidance, and if students have difficulty the teacher resumes more responsibility and models again. Third, the strategy the support teaches is placed on an explicit trade-off — narrow prescriptive strategies ensure success but do not transfer, broad ones transfer but are vague and hard to teach — which is the review's central tension stated plainly in 1995. The report measures nothing, twice reports that the reviewed literature supplied no example for a cell of its own matrix, and fills those cells with author-written illustrations.

medium · A translation document, not a study. No data, no sample, no statistics and no effect sizes of any kind across 26 pages, and it does not re-read the primary literature: it takes the studies already assembled in a separate synthesis by the same three authors and sorts their teaching techniques into six principles borrowed from a 1992 curriculum-design monograph by colleagues at the same centre. Most instructional detail is third-hand, reaching the reader through a review of a review, so the chain from a described classroom procedure back to an observation is long and unverifiable here. Against that, the conceptual content is explicit and is the reason to hold the card: the four-carrier definition of scaffolding, the different ending given to each carrier, the two-directional contingency rule and the specificity-against-transfer trade-off are all stated in the authors' own voice as principles. They also mark two cells of their own matrix as unsupported by the reviewed literature and fill them with invented examples, which bounds the framework honestly. Treat the concepts as evidence about how this tradition thought; treat every reported instructional effect as hearsay.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: One definition, four carriers of support, and — read closely — three different endings, which the authors do not remark on. Support carried by a person is faded as fluency grows. Support carried by content and by tasks is never withdrawn at all: what the authors call content and task scaffolding is a difficulty ladder, so the thing that changes over time is the work, not the help, and when the ladder ends there is nothing to remove. Support carried by materials is kept until the student can apply the knowledge independently — a competence criterion, stated without any way of establishing that the competence has arrived. For this review the split is worth more than the definition. It says that when a paper reports that scaffolding was faded, the sentence can mean a person easing off, a curriculum getting harder, or a handout left available indefinitely, and only the first is withdrawal in the sense the tradition intends. It also explains a pattern seen elsewhere in this corpus: tool papers default to permanent support partly because the supports they build are of the material kind, whose stated ending is a condition nobody checks rather than a schedule anybody runs.

quotes: Mediated scaffolding is the external support provided by teacher/peers, content, tasks, and materials during initial instruction in the conventions of text presentation and organizational patterns of text structures. Scaffolding occurs across and within lessons (Duffy & Roehler, 1989) as teachers weave together the various types of scaffolding to facilitate student learning and independent performance. Among the four types of mediated scaffolding discussed here, teacher/peer scaffolding occurs across a continuum, with more support occurring when new concepts, tasks, or strategies are introduced. Support is then faded as students gain fluency and assume more responsibility. Content and task scaffolding occur by proceeding from easier to more difficult content or tasks. However, at times, content and tasks are held constant as students learn and practice new strategies or procedures. Finally, material scaffolding guides students' thinking as they acquire new concepts, skills, or strategies. Students maintain access to scaffolded materials until they are able to apply the new knowledge independently

rows.value: (PDF p. 14) Mediated scaffolding defined: four carriers, four different endings — This is the most useful paragraph in the report because it splits scaffolding by what carries the support and then gives each carrier a different ending, in one breath and apparently without noticing. Teacher and peer support is faded as fluency grows. Content and task scaffolding is not withdrawn at all: it is a difficulty ladder, so what changes over time is the task, not the help, and there is nothing left to take away when the ladder ends. Material scaffolding is retained until the student can work without it, which is a competence criterion rather than a schedule. Three different withdrawal regimes are therefore filed under one word. For a review trying to say what fading means, that is a warning: a paper that reports scaffolding faded may be describing a person easing off, a curriculum getting harder, or a handout that stays on the desk indefinitely, and only the first is withdrawal in the sense the tradition intends.
quotes: Mediated scaffolding is the external support provided by teacher/peers, content, tasks, and materials during initial instruction in the conventions of text presentation and organizational patterns of text structures. Scaffolding occurs across and within lessons (Duffy & Roehler, 1989) as teachers weave together the various types of scaffolding to facilitate student learning and independent performance. Among the four types of mediated scaffolding discussed here, teacher/peer scaffolding occurs across a continuum, with more support occurring when new concepts, tasks, or strategies are introduced. Support is then faded as students gain fluency and assume more responsibility. Content and task scaffolding occur by proceeding from easier to more difficult content or tasks. However, at times, content and tasks are held constant as students learn and practice new strategies or procedures. Finally, material scaffolding guides students' thinking as they acquire new concepts, skills, or strategies. Students maintain access to scaffolded materials until they are able to apply the new knowledge independently

rows.value: low · The definition and the three endings are stated explicitly in the authors' own voice in a single paragraph, so what the paper says is not in doubt. What is uncertain is only whether the distinction holds up empirically, and the report offers nothing on that.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: Withdrawal here is contingent, and unusually it runs in both directions. The trigger for reducing support is observed proficiency; the trigger for restoring it is observed difficulty; a wrong answer gets modelling and a half-right answer gets a guiding question. The same person makes every call, inside the lesson, from what the child just did. That matters because contingent withdrawal is close to absent everywhere else in this corpus — a scoping review of 32 experimental studies of online argumentation scaffolding found none, and the strongest fading experiment in the corpus ran a fixed 9:1 to 1:9 ratio identical for every learner. The obstacle has always been named as diagnosis: you cannot withdraw contingently without knowing what the learner can now do. This report shows the diagnosis in its cheapest form, a teacher watching a child fail to name a story problem, which is exactly what an instrumented system does not have. Two limits are severe. Nothing here is measured: this is a procedure the authors report from cited studies, and there is no observation of how often teachers actually re-escalate, no fidelity check, and no outcome. And the re-escalation rule applies only to the teacher-carried support; nothing in the report lets content, tasks or materials respond to a struggling student.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: This review's central tension, written down in 1995, and located in an unusual place: not in how a support was evaluated but in how specific its content was made. Specificity buys performance now and costs reach later; generality buys reach and costs teachability. That is the same shape as a tool improving every measure it computes and none it does not, and the same shape as good retention with poor transfer, but one level upstream of both — the trade-off is designed into the support before anyone measures anything. It is a genuine design-space dimension: where on the specificity axis a support sits is a choice, and the report gives worked examples at the chosen midpoint, such as a four-question problem-solution-effect routine with a three-column notesheet, which the authors say transfers to social studies text not written in that structure. The weakness is that the resolution is asserted. No definition of middle-range is given, no test distinguishes it from narrow, and the supporting citations are two secondary syntheses rather than a comparison of strategies at different breadths. Carry the trade-off, not the answer.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The report is organised as a matrix — five procedural principles crossed with two content areas — and every cell has confident instructional prose in it. Twice the authors state that the reviewed literature contained nothing for a cell, and then write the cell anyway from their own judgement, signalled only by the word However. Read that as the general condition of design-principle frameworks rather than as a defect of this one: the prose in an evidenced cell is stylistically identical to the prose in an invented cell, so a later reader mining such a framework for evidence inherits recommendations of two entirely different kinds under one heading. What makes this document unusually trustworthy is precisely that it marks the seam, which most frameworks do not. The same reading applies to the report's evidential base overall. There is exactly one outcome comparison in 26 pages, reported at third hand — recall on uninstructed texts on the same topics beat answering questions or extra study — with no sample, design, interval or statistic; everything else is a description of a procedure. So the framework's authority comes from its coherence and its institutional provenance, not from evidence a reader can inspect.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: Scaffolding arrives here through curriculum design, not through developmental psychology, and the difference is visible in the vocabulary. Across 26 pages the word scaffold appears 33 times; Vygotsky, zone of proximal development, contingency, withdrawal and the noun fading appear zero times, and the verb faded appears once. The sources are a 1992 monograph on curriculum guidelines from the same centre, a 1989 chapter on strategy instruction, and reading-comprehension reviews. Scaffolding is one principle among six, listed between conspicuous strategies and strategic integration and no more central than judicious review — which is to say it is a property of a curriculum here, not a relationship between two people. Put this next to the fifty-four-page Vygotskian thesis in this corpus that uses Vygotsky 136 times, scaffolding 44 and fading zero, and the pair settles a lineage question from both ends: neither tradition carries the other's vocabulary, and a paper that says scaffold without saying Vygotsky is not being careless, it is in the other line of descent. The practical consequence for this review is that searching for contingency and fading will systematically miss the instructional-design half of the literature, which discusses the same operations under handover, proficiency, independent application and firming.

cards.title: Programming as problem solving: a participatory theater approach

rows.value: S2W-9ECB242BAE61D0FBA4496078
other
framework or design space, design principle, concept or theory

A 1994 paper from the Colorado group that gives the corpus something it badly needs: a continuous axis for how much of the work a system does, with the position on it set moment by moment by the person rather than by a schedule. The two ends are direct manipulation, where the user is holding hand puppets and must do everything themselves, and complete delegation, where the script has been written, the play has started, and the audience watches. The proposal in between is participatory theater: actors follow their script unless the audience tells them otherwise, so that if the user does not participate they are a passive observer and if they participate excessively they have taken the production over completely — and moving between those states requires no mode, no restart, no explicit run-interact-stop cycle. It also carries a distinction worth stealing. A critiquing system holds evaluative knowledge only: it tells the designer something is wrong, and the same message comes back whether the kitchen work triangle is 24 feet or 2400. The alternative represents the same rule as a degree of fit, which can drive movement — kitchen appliances that shuffle themselves towards better positions, so the rule is never stated and can only be felt by pushing against it. Nobody is studied. There are no participants, no measures and no results anywhere in ten pages.

high · There is no evidence about people in this paper at all. Five principles are derived by argument from Simon, Schoen, Fischer, Green and Nardi, then illustrated by walking through three systems the authors built. No study is reported, no participant appears, no task is timed and no outcome is counted. The nearest thing to a result is a claim that a mixed team built a substantial voice-dialog design environment in under four months and revised it in response to user evaluations, both citing other papers, plus a count that the substrate had produced over forty applications in four years — which is evidence about the substrate's reach and not about anyone using it. So carry the vocabulary and the distinctions, which are sharp, original for their date, and still unmatched in this corpus for describing partial delegation. Carry nothing about benefit. Where the paper does describe user experience — that the kitchen work triangle can be indirectly experienced by pushing appliances around — it is the designers' account of what their system affords, not an observation of anybody doing it.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A continuous axis for how much of the work a system does, with the position on it set by the person, moment to moment, in 1994. Almost every support in this corpus is binary — present or absent, on a schedule someone else wrote — and the few that vary do so in discrete steps chosen by a designer. Here the quantity is the user's own level of participation, and the two poles are named precisely enough to be useful: at one end you are holding hand puppets, in complete control and doing everything yourself, bounded by the sequentiality of single human actions; at the other the script is written, the play has started, and you are watching. Three properties transfer. The axis is continuous, so there is no threshold anywhere on it. It is set by behaviour rather than by declaration, so nobody has to decide in advance how much help is wanted. And crossing it costs nothing: because the same channels serve the user and the system, a person can interject an action or redirect the script without stopping anything, and the authors state explicitly that no run-interact-stop cycle is needed. That last point is the one modern systems still get wrong, since asking to change how much a tool does usually means opening a settings panel. What the axis does not contain is any notion of the position changing over weeks, or of anyone deciding it should.

Excessive participation will result in the user taking over the production completely to the point of direct manipulation.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The cleanest statement in this corpus of a distinction that decides what a support can do for someone. A support carrying evaluative knowledge can only tell you that you are wrong; a support carrying constructive knowledge encodes the same rule as a gradient and can therefore say which way is better. The example is unimprovable: a kitchen critic checking that the stove, sink and refrigerator lie within 23 feet of each other returns the identical message at 24 feet and at 2400 feet, because a predicate has nowhere to put the difference. Recast as a degree of fit, the same rule becomes a direction, and the appliances can walk towards it. Three consequences are worth carrying. A boolean support can only interrupt, so it is confined to the moments when something has already gone wrong, which is why critiquing systems feel like alarms. A graded support can act, which is what makes automation possible at all, and this paper is candid that acting is what it does — the appliances rearrange themselves. And the same recasting is what allows the user to steer, since the three interventions the paper offers all operate on the gradient rather than on the verdict: push an agent out of a local maximum, alter the landscape, or change how happiness is measured.

rows.value: As such, critic rules only explicitly represent evaluative knowledge; they notify designers that something is wrong but provide no constructive knowledge about how to remedy the situation... Evaluative knowledge typically consists of predicates returning a true or false value based on the current situation. For instance, the work triangle critic returns the same notification message to the designer regardless of whether the total distance is 24 feet or 2400 feet. However, hill-climbing agents provide a different knowledge representation of this same work triangle situation that returns a degree of fit. This result is used to constructively drive the hill climbing process.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A support that never states what it knows. The work triangle rule is nowhere in the interface; the user encounters it only as resistance, by trying to put the sink somewhere and watching the room push back. This is the far end of an axis this corpus has been assembling from both directions — the pole where a support conceals what it stands in for, against the pole where the goal is to expose complexity so the user can take control of it — and the interesting thing is that here concealment is not a trick played on the user but a claim about how spatial knowledge is best conveyed. The paper's own framing is that a critic tells you and a landscape lets you feel, and that feeling is better. Whether anyone ends up able to lay out a kitchen unaided is not asked, and could not be answered by anything in the paper. What redeems the design is the override, which is more sophisticated than most modern equivalents: the user does not simply accept or reject the system's move but can weaken a specific guideline or freeze a specific component, so the support's authority is adjustable both by rule and by object. The authors are also honest that the arrangement produces conflict between what the user wants and what the guidelines want, which is a more candid description of automated assistance than most papers manage.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The design property that makes the whole spectrum work also destroys the record of who did what. Because a user's action and an agent's action travel the same channels, a person can step into a running simulation without stopping it — the example given is adding insects to an area where the frogs are starving instead of waiting for them to die and starting over — and by the same token the system cannot tell afterwards which insects came from the person. The authors report this as a virtue and it is one: seamlessness is exactly what symmetry buys. But it is worth recording as a measurement hazard, because it is the structural opposite of designs that keep provenance visible so the user can see which values are the system's default and which are their own override. A system with symmetric communication cannot produce a log that attributes work, which means the division of labour between person and machine — the thing an evaluation of a support most needs to see — is unrecoverable in principle rather than merely unrecorded. Any modern system that lets an assistant and a user edit the same document through the same interface has inherited this problem, usually without noticing.

In both cases, the same sensors and effecters are used... cards.title: PEOPLE POWER - A HUMAN-COMPUTER COLLABORATIVE LEARNING-SYSTEM

rows.value: S2W-D70D7CC14D150060BC3FE48D
other
concept or theory, primary empirical, framework or design space, failure or counterevidence

A 1992 system and a computational theory of how talking with someone becomes thinking by yourself. The learner and an artificial partner called Jerry Mander share a micro-world of electoral systems and argue about which ward to move to win seats. The theory has three postulates: an individual is a society of communicating agents, a pair is the same society split across two bodies, and because communication between bodies is visible to both, patterns of argument formed between people are reused inside one. The implementation makes that literal. One procedure takes a proposer and a criticiser; give it two learners and it produces dialogue, give it one learner twice and it produces reasoning. Refutations worked out with a partner become extra conditions on the learner's own rules. The design is also deliberately not expert: the partner starts no more knowledgeable than the learner, has no hidden knowledge and no teaching intention, and what it acquires is not facts but the organisation of facts. The trial went badly and the authors say why. Five people used it for an hour, found the cost of each exchange high, and so talked less; the partner learns only from exchanges, so it stayed weak, giving poor suggestions, which reduced interest further. Their dialogue networks reached fewer than ten links where twenty-five is where the machine-to-machine version starts working. Two participants said taking part forced them into the machine's logic.

medium · The theoretical contribution is the strong part and it is unusually disciplined: three stated postulates, a representation making the individual and the pair the same object, and an implementation in which reasoning and dialogue are literally one procedure with different arguments. That is a testable commitment rather than a metaphor, and the authors say plainly that the ideas are Vygotsky's, Piaget's and Mead's and that their contribution is making them consistent enough to build. The empirical side carries very little. Five subjects for one hour, reported through appreciation and feelings; the one number is that their dialogue networks held under ten links against a working threshold of about twenty-five taken from machine-to-machine runs whose full report sits outside the paper. Nothing measures whether any human internalised anything, which is the mechanism the model is about. The failure analysis is the most reliable thing here because it is specific and self-implicating: the authors name the interaction cost, trace the spiral it caused and state the condition it implies. Carry the model and the failure; carry no effect.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A mechanism for how external support becomes internal capability, stated precisely enough to build and then built. The claim is that thinking and conversing are the same operation differently partitioned, so a pattern of argument formed between two people can be replayed inside one; the implementation makes it a calling convention, with one procedure producing dialogue when its proposer and criticiser are different agents and reasoning when they are the same agent twice. Most of this corpus asserts that support leaves something behind and measures nothing about it. Here the residue is named exactly: alone, the learner can refute itself only with refutations that were elaborated jointly, so what collaboration deposits is the set of objections you would not have raised on your own. That also explains why a partner is needed rather than more practice, since the objection has to come from somewhere. Two things bound it. The dialogue supports two moves, accept and refute, which the authors name as their main limitation. And the account is a model of a process, validated by being implementable, not by being observed in a person.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: A failure with a loop in it, reported by the authors against their own system. Each exchange was expensive, so people had fewer of them; the partner improves only through exchanges, so it stayed weak; a weak partner is not worth talking to, so there were fewer exchanges still. The numbers make it concrete rather than rhetorical: an hour of human use produced patterns under ten links where the machine-to-machine version needs about twenty-five to work. What generalises is the shape. Any support that gets better through use and costs effort to use can fall into this spiral, and a support that starts below the threshold where it is worth engaging never gets above it. The authors draw the right conclusion, that a collaborating partner needs some minimum competence before collaboration is viable, which is a genuine boundary on the no-more-knowledgeable-than-the-learner premise the same paper argues for. It is five people for one hour, and the threshold comes from machine-to-machine runs whose report sits outside the paper, so the mechanism is worth more than the number.

rows.value: Because the cost of interaction was very high, subjects reduced the number of interactions. Since Jerry's learning output depends directly of the amount of interactions, Jerry has been learning slowly. All dialogue patterns elaborated by Jerry during these one-hour sessions included less than 10 inter-agents links, while dialogue patterns built in experiments with two artificial learners become efficient around 25 links. Hence, Jerry continued to provide the learners with suggestions that were not very good, and hence decreased the subjects interest in its suggestions. The co-learner must possess some minimal skills to maintain the learner's interest in collaboration.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A support designed to add structure without adding content, argued explicitly against the tutor-as-expert position. The partner holds no facts the learner lacks, keeps nothing hidden, and has no teaching intention; what it contributes is the arrangement of things both parties already know into chains and objections. That matters for this review because it is one of the few designs in the corpus that cannot substitute for the person's own knowledge even in principle. Set beside the decision-support tradition of the same period, which ranks advice systems by how strong a theory of the domain they embed and treats a user who need not reason as the achievement, this is the opposite parameter setting on the same axis. The design also makes the commitment concrete in three places: knowledge is inspectable rather than hidden, the partner asks questions to get answers rather than to test, and disagreement resolves in the human's favour, since she may hold her position when it objects while it abandons its own when she disproves it. The price is paid in the trial: a partner that starts weak may never become worth talking to.

The acquired expertise is the organisation of these rules into patterns.

cards.title: The structure of design problem spaces

rows.value: other
framework or design space, concept or theory, primary empirical

A cognitive-science account of what makes design a distinct kind of problem solving, built from twelve verbal protocols by working designers in architecture, mechanical engineering and instructional design, three analysed in detail and compared against nondesign protocols such as cryptarithmetic. The argument runs from the task environment to the head: because design problems are underspecified, have no right or wrong answers, and return no genuine feedback from the world during the session, the designer must supply the missing structure, simulate the feedback, and use evaluation functions and stopping rules that are personal and acquired by immersion in the profession. Twelve invariants follow, of which the load-bearing ones for this review are the personalised stopping rule, the monotonic incremental development of ideas that are almost never discarded, the decomposition into leaky rather than clean modules, and the heavy use of external models and artificial symbol systems. The one quantified pattern of a support falling away is not about help at all: the client and the design brief supply roughly half of what is said while the problem is being structured and have disappeared by the detailing phase, with the designer's own knowledge running the rest.

medium · The framework is the durable part and is argued carefully: each of the twelve invariants is derived from a stated feature of the task environment plus a stated constraint on the information-processing system, and the paper is explicit that they are predictions about which tasks will and will not show them. The design-versus-nondesign contrast is the strongest empirical move, and the surviving numbers are stark: problem structuring at about a quarter of design statements against 0.3 percent in nondesign, interconnection density at 7.4 percent against 20 percent for cryptarithmetic. The sample is what limits it. Twelve protocols were collected, three analysed, and the interconnection and control-structure results rest on one architecture subject; the nondesign protocols came from the literature rather than matched collection; every contrast is descriptive, not tested. There are no novices, so nothing says how any of this is acquired. Carry the framework as a characterisation of the work, and the percentages as illustrations from a handful of protocols rather than population estimates.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is the cleanest statement in the corpus of why support in design work resists evaluation. The world returns nothing while the work is happening; the designer generates the feedback. Add that there are no right or wrong answers and the consequence follows: whatever tells a designer how they are doing is a construction, not a reading, and the quality of that construction is what the expertise consists of. The stopping rule and the evaluation function are, on this account, derived from immersion in a profession — which is to say they are the part a novice lacks and years install. A support that supplies feedback here, or that decides when the work is good enough, is therefore not relieving a chore; it is doing the thing the profession is, and its absence in the person cannot be detected by inspecting the artifact, because the artifact has no correct version to be compared against. That gives the dependence findings elsewhere in this corpus a mechanism stated at the level of the task environment, decades before the tools that would make it urgent. It also explains why so many studies here score outcomes with instruments their own authors built: in this class of work there is nothing else to score against.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the only curve in the paper that looks like a support falling away, and it pays to be exact about what it is. The design brief and the client carry a large share of what gets said while the problem is being structured, still supply something at preliminary design, and have disappeared by the detailing phase, with the designer's own knowledge carrying essentially all of it by then. Nobody withdrew anything. The designer stopped consulting the source, on their own timing, because the information had been brought into the problem space and there was nothing further to fetch. That is a third regime beside fixed-schedule fading and contingent diagnosis: an external information source that is used up rather than removed, its decline set by the phase of the work. It also shows the limits of reading such a curve as evidence of anything. Consultation falling to zero is equally consistent with the brief having been absorbed and with the designer having simply stopped checking against it, and this design cannot separate them; there is no measurement after the session at all. Any modern tool that reports declining use of its help panel as evidence of growing independence is making exactly this inference, on exactly this evidence.

quotes: Problem structuring is the process of drawing upon our knowledge to com- pensate for missing information and using this knowledge to construct the problem space (Simon, 1973a). Design problems are incompletely specified but the specification of a problem space requires complete information about start states, goal states, operators, and evaluation functions. In Goel and Pirolli (1989) we examined the form and organization of some of this knowledge and how it was applied. items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The twelve invariants are a design space for the work rather than for the support, and that is what makes them useful here: they say what a tool entering this kind of work is entering. Two of them constrain instrument design directly. Decomposition is dictated by the designer's own practice and experience rather than by the problem, so a support that imposes a decomposition — a template, a fixed set of sections, a prescribed sequence of steps — is asserting a structure the task does not carry, and differences between people in where they cut the problem are signal rather than noise. And the modules are leaky rather than clean, at 7.4 percent of possible interconnections against 20 percent for cryptarithmetic, which is the quantitative form of the same point: the designer's freedom to attend to some connections and ignore others is what keeps a large problem tractable, so a tool that enforces consistency across all of them removes the mechanism that makes the work possible. The contrast class matters too. The paper is explicit that these features do not hold where constraints are logical and constitutive of the problem, which is exactly the kind of task most tutoring and scaffolding research uses.

Because the problems only had six columns, there were only six modules (as compared to over 30 for each of the design tasks). items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Monotonic incremental development is a hard constraint on what a support may do to work in progress, and the reason given is structural rather than habitual: with no right or wrong answers there is little basis for abandoning a partial solution, so ideas are retained and massaged rather than replaced. A tool that answers a request by generating a fresh alternative instead of developing what is already on the page is working against the control structure the task has. The nondesign contrast makes the point sharply — in problem spaces where most explored paths are wrong, abandoning a path is the correct move and the knowledge attached to it is rightly discarded. Supports built on that second model and deployed in the first will feel to their users like they keep resetting the work, which is a testable prediction this paper supplies and nobody in this corpus has tested. The same invariant also explains why designers accumulate rather than converge, and therefore why a stopping rule has to come from the person: nothing in the accumulating artifact will ever announce that it is finished.

cards.title: Getting advice from a computer: five models and a simulator

rows.value: other
framework or design space, concept or theory, measurement or method

A 1991 management-information-systems article that sorts computer advice-giving into five kinds by how strong a theory the system holds: none at all, so the advice is just how things look; a data model, so the advice is a query result; a similarity model, so the advice is what happened in comparable past cases; a logical model, so the advice is an implication; and a causal model, so the advice is a calculated payoff. The scale is explicitly two-sided, ordered by how much help the person gets and by how much knowledge somebody had to have in order to build the model. What makes it worth carrying is that the author names the quantity moving in the other direction. As the model gets stronger the user's share of the work shrinks, from puzzling out what a report means, to judging whether past cases really are similar, to nothing: at the top of the scale the paper says situations must be described exactly, the theory must relate causes to effects uniquely, and users can be quite unintelligent. That is written as an achievement. Set against it is a prediction the paper makes and does not test, that the stronger modes should lose to the weaker ones until their models are valid, with the crossover arriving later in harder domains. A simulator, CARMART, was built to test that; the study is described and its results are not reported.

low · There are no results here. The article states a taxonomy, describes a simulator built to test it, gives five hypotheses and two predicted interaction plots, and reports that undergraduate management classes are currently being used as subjects. Nothing is measured. The single empirical datum is a prior field study of thirty respondents whose relationship the author calls weak, and whose actual finding runs against the hypothesis it was meant to support. The taxonomy itself is asserted rather than derived from any sample of systems, and the ordering criterion, the power of the embedded theory, is the author's own. There is also a boundary the paper does not mark: inside the simulator a valid model means one that matches a hidden payoff formula the designer wrote, so validity there is agreement with a known ground truth rather than correspondence to a world. Carry the taxonomy, the intelligence-shifts-to-the-system observation and the untested crossover prediction as ideas; carry nothing here as evidence.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A design-space dimension for supports, stated in 1991 and outside the education literature, which is why it is worth having: it orders systems by how strong a theory of the domain they hold, from none, so the advice is just an appearance, through a data model, a similarity model and a logical model, to a causal model that computes the answer. The axis is not complexity or interactivity or intelligence in the marketing sense; it is how much of the domain has been formalised before the person arrives, and that is a property any support has. The paper also gives the axis a price, which most design spaces do not: each step up requires somebody to have possessed and encoded more knowledge, so the scale simultaneously measures what the user gets and what a designer had to know. It is asserted rather than derived from any survey of systems, and the five levels are the author's own cut, but as a way of placing supports beside one another it transfers directly to the tools this review is concerned with, where the same range runs from a highlighted diff to a system that writes the answer.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The most useful paragraph in the article, because it makes the trade explicit. As the system's model gets stronger, the reasoning left to the person shrinks, and the author tracks it: at the weak end the user must work out what a query result means, in the middle they must judge whether the retrieved cases are genuinely similar and whether the similarity criteria were the right ones, and at the strong end there is nothing left to judge because the theory resolves the situation uniquely. So intelligence behaves like a conserved quantity moving from person to system. What makes this worth carrying is the sign the author puts on it. Users can be quite unintelligent is written as a capability of the system, an achievement, and the article never asks what it costs. There is no question about whether such a user could conclude without the system, whether they would notice a wrong causal model, or what happens over time. That is a clean 1991 statement of the position this review keeps finding implicitly: the goal of support is to make the person's own competence unnecessary, and the consequences of succeeding are not part of the design problem.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A contingency claim about supports in general, and a good one, stated precisely enough to be wrong. A more powerful support is not simply better: it needs a valid model, building one costs time and knowledge, that cost rises with how hard the domain is, and until it is paid the weaker support outperforms the stronger. So the ordering of supports by power inverts at short horizons and in hard domains, and the crossover point is a quantity worth knowing. This is the shape of finding this review wants and it has been rediscovered repeatedly since, in exactly the form where a system that supplies more produces worse early performance than one that supplies less. The trouble is that here it is a prediction with two plotted figures and no data. The study is described in the present tense, classes are being run, and no result is reported anywhere in the article. There is also a boundary the author does not draw: in the simulator a valid model means one matching a hidden formula with a known number of non-interacting factors, so model-building there is a much easier problem than in any real domain, which if anything makes the predicted delays conservative.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: A second contingency axis, and one this review sees less often: which support is wanted depends on where the person is in the task rather than on who the person is. The five stages given are pre-conclusion, investigation, representation, interpretation and post-conclusion, and the proposal is that different kinds of advice become salient at different ones. It is a reasonable idea and the article's own evidence is against it in an interesting way. Thirty respondents were asked, and every one of them wanted case-based consulting help at every stage, which is why the relationship came out weak. That pattern suggests something other than stage-matching drives demand: people want a precedent whatever they are doing. The author reports this plainly rather than burying it, and reads it as needing further work. Thirty self-reports cannot settle the question either way, but as a small piece of negative evidence it is worth keeping, because the same pull toward whatever support answers with a concrete instance shows up elsewhere in this corpus.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: A definition of support built entirely around reaching an outcome. There are two states in it, the situation before and the conclusion after, and the whole value of the support lies in moving between them. No third state exists in which the person is different afterwards, and none is wanted: the article is explicit that advice covers learning as one of several possible conclusions and then narrows to information-processing without, it says, affecting the generality. Read against the education-side definitions in this corpus, the contrast is exact. There a support is for a learner and is meant to become unnecessary; here it is for a concluder and is meant to work. Across the whole article the words scaffold, fading, fade, withdraw, novice and expertise occur zero times, verified by folding every page to lowercase alphanumerics and counting substrings, while depend occurs seven times, all of it about which advice suits which situation. So the vocabulary of contingency is present and the vocabulary of withdrawal is entirely absent, which is what it looks like when the same design problem is approached without the developmental tradition.

cards.title: Artificial neural networks as cognitive tools for professional writing

rows.value: other
concept or theory, design principle, framework or design space

A 1990 position paper with three unevaluated prototypes, arguing that computer-aided writing tools had gone wrong by measuring surface features after the fact and treating all text alike, and that neural networks could give holistic assessments instead. Nobody used any of the three, no data is reported, the third is admitted to lack a large enough training set, and one figure is labelled hypothetical. What makes it worth a card is the vocabulary. Carlson uses scaffolding once, in scare quotes, with no citation, as the thing that makes a system a tutor rather than a tool: because of the amount of scaffolding each writing environment provides, they seem more appropriate as a learning environment, and in short they are more tutors than tools. For a professional writer, on her account, support is a liability. She then argues, four pages later, that the reason to externalise the writing process is that its abstractness keeps people from forming the strategies necessary for expert behaviour. She also states a feedback-order principle worth carrying: commentary should start with a holistic appraisal, then say what features drove it, then say how to change the result. And she warns that new tools engender new habits of mind, so the tool over time can change the nature of the task.

low · There is no evidence here of any kind. No participant used any of the three prototypes, no measurement is reported, no comparison is run and no claim about an effect on a writer is tested. Of the three, the first automates an existing hand-scored instrument, the second was built with the data hand-processed for both the training set and the test cases, and the third is stated by the author to lack a training set large enough for meaningful results, with its figure explicitly labelled hypothetical data. The critique of existing tools is asserted from the author's own experience of using them, in the first person. What the paper is good for is its vocabulary and its stated principles, which are precise, unusual, and datable to 1990: the tutor-versus-tool line drawn by amount of scaffolding, the ordering rule for feedback, the backchaining requirement, and the warning that tools change tasks. Cite it as a position and a lineage marker, never as a result.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A 1990 sighting of the word doing a job the modern literature rarely gives it. Carlson is separating a learning environment from a professional tool, and the axis she separates them on is quantity of scaffolding: past some amount of support a system stops being a tool and becomes a tutor, and for a working writer that is a defect. Three things transfer. The distinction itself is the review's design-space question, and it is one of the few places anyone states it as an axis rather than assuming a population. The polarity is unusual and worth recording, because most of this corpus treats more support as more help; here more support is a reason to reject the system. And the philology matters: the word appears exactly once in sixteen pages, in scare quotes, with no citation to Wood, Bruner and Ross, no Vygotsky, and no mention of contingency, fading or transfer of responsibility anywhere in the paper. By 1990 the term had already reached professional-writing computing as a loose quantity meaning amount of guidance provided, stripped of every mechanism that made it a scaffold. What Carlson does not consider is the possibility the original construct was built for: a system that provides a lot of support and then provides less.
