items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: A stated sequence for feedback, which is rarer and more useful than a stated quantity. Verdict first, then the evidence behind the verdict, then the action; and the diagnosis it answers has three separable parts that are still the standard complaints about automated writing feedback thirty-five years later. Two of them deserve separating. Grain: an assessment pitched at surface features is not merely less useful, it redirects the writer, and Carlson names the harm directly, that writers become obsessed with surface errors rather than with strengthening logic and content. That is the same shape as the finding elsewhere in this corpus that gains land on whatever the tool can score. Timing: after-the-fact profiling arrives when the decisions have been made, which makes the support an audit rather than a collaborator. The third, treating all text as equal, is a claim that a support must be indexed to the genre and purpose of the document, and it is the one Carlson does least about. None of this is tested; it is a practitioner's design rule, and it is worth carrying as a specification a later study could evaluate rather than as a result.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The support delivers a verdict and then opens the verdict up, and the stated reason is that the writer may not accept it. That places this paper at the transparent pole of the corpus, directly opposite embedded scaffolding built so that users are less likely to notice it is there. Three properties are worth separating. The support assesses and does not act, so the artifact stays the writer's. Its reasoning is inspectable at the level at which the writer can do something about it, which is the useful sense of explanation and is much narrower than the usual sense. And disagreement is designed in: the sentence assumes a writer who is not satisfied with the result and gives her the handle to overturn it, rather than treating non-compliance as error. Set against the paper's tutor-versus-tool line, this is what Carlson means by a tool. The limitation is that inspectability is offered as a property of the interface and never checked against anything: whether writers backchain, whether they overturn verdicts they should, or whether exposing sixteen weights simply moves the obsession with surface features one level down is not asked.

rows.value: "An added benefit is the ability to 'backchain' -- that is, given the three dimensions of the end profile, the writer can backtrack and find out which of the sixteen elements were more heavily weighted in determining the stylistic evaluation. Thus, if the writer were not satisfied with the result, she would know what textual features to work on to produce a different, more agreeable, final analysis."

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: An argument against building a support on a fixed model of the work, made from the history of technology rather than from psychology, and the reasoning is that the support will alter the thing it was designed against. Two uses. As a design principle it is a case for looseness: a support whose model of the task is committed and integrated will be wrong later in a way a loosely coupled set of tools will not, because the tool's own presence moves the target. As a methodological warning it bears on every evaluation in this corpus, since a study measuring a support against the task as it was before the support existed is measuring a task that is on its way out. The claim converges with Tikhomirov's, that moving routine components to a machine includes the machine in a social role and fundamentally transforms the content of that role. Neither author cites the other or any shared source, and they arrive from opposite directions, one from Soviet activity theory and one from the history of technology. Two independent arrivals is a reason to take the proposition seriously; neither supplies a case, a measurement or a mechanism, which is a reason not to treat it as established.

cards.title: The role of external representation in the writing process: implications for the design of hypertext-based writing tools

rows.value: other
concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle, lineage or history, measurement or method

External representation here means something precise and dated: a structure held on paper or a screen, analysed inside Anderson's production-system architecture of a single mind. Not distributed cognition, which did not yet have that name, and not cognitive load. The paper takes Bobrow's definition of a representation as a selective mapping from a world, then borrows Simon's informational equivalence and Larkin and Simon's computational equivalence to ask a question the field had left open: when is one external representation better than another? The answer is eight criteria, each naming a cognitive process the representation relieves. What it takes over is retrieval, because a thing kept in sight stays active and never has to be fetched; the storage of intermediate results; the current goal; and the goals a writer has suspended and means to return to. What it does not take over is learning. The paper cites Craik to say that keeping an element in working memory longer does not decide whether it is stored permanently, so a representation you can see is not a thing you will know. The tools built on this, Notes and a Summary Graph, Synthesis Grid and Synthesis Tree, supply slots drawn from the schema the paper's experts were observed using, and the writer fills them; an empty cell is meant to show the writer a source position they never noticed. Only Notes was implemented. Nothing here is evaluated, and the authors say the field had only informal evaluations to go on. The process model underneath comes from thinking-aloud protocols of five experts and two novices, which they call preliminary and, on the hierarchy step, suggestive but far from conclusive.

high · Read everything here as a proposal with cited support. Nothing in this paper is measured, three of its four tools did not exist yet, and its own process model rests on seven subjects the authors describe as too few. The value is in three things that are hard to get elsewhere: an exact statement of which account of external representation is being used and what follows from it, a list of the cognitive functions a representation actually takes over, and a null saying that visibility is not learning, which the authors report even though it works against their own design.

sections.title: 8 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.small: concept or lineage, principle, open question
items.lead: This is the theoretical line the review sits on, and it is worth being exact about which line it is. The paper does not use distributed cognition, which had not been named, and it does not use cognitive load. It uses Anderson's architecture, and the consequence is that external representation is analysed as relief for a single mind's memory and control, not as thinking spread across people and things. That turns out to be the more useful frame for the question this review asks, because it forces the answer to be specific: not that a display helps, but which process it relieves. The eight criteria are still a usable checklist, and they are more discriminating than most of what the corpus offers, because two of them are about attention and encoding, three about memory, and three about goals, and a support that helps with one of these does not thereby help with the others. What is missing is the reverse: there is no criterion for what a representation costs the person who uses it, and the only such cost in the paper arrives as someone else's finding.

rows.value: Although external representations have occupied a central place in hypertext research, little is known about what makes one better than another, and competing representations have received only informal evaluations. Drawing on an architectural model of human cognition, the paper develops a framework for answering the question when is one external representation better than another, yielding eight criteria stated in terms of encoding, storage and retrieval, match and execution, and the control of cognition. The framework is intended as a foundation for more formal evaluations, though it does not itself generate user interfaces for tasks.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The most transferable idea in the paper, and the one that gives the review a way to talk about form without hand-waving. Two supports that say the same thing are not the same support, and the difference is measured in inferences the person no longer has to make. That is a real account of what a structure does: it does not add information, it converts an inference into a perception. It is worth holding onto the third cited result as well, because it is the counterweight: the same sensitivity that lets a good layout do this lets a bad one break the chunks a reader would otherwise have formed, and recall fell. So the claim is not that explicit structure is good, it is that surface form has leverage in both directions. The weakness is provenance. None of these results are the authors', none involve writing or any extended task, and the paper reports them as directions with no numbers at all.

rows.value: Two representations are informationally equivalent if all the information in one is inferable from the other and vice versa, but they may not be computationally equivalent: the processes that operate on them do not carry out those operations with equivalent ease and speed. This inequivalence significantly influences problem-solving performance. Subjects operating with a verbal representation, in which a relationship is not explicitly represented, fail to make the inferences necessary to discover the crucial relationships, while subjects operating with a diagrammatic representation do not need to infer the relationship, since it is represented explicitly.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: This is the paper's answer to the question the review keeps asking, and it is unusually precise. The representation takes over four things and they are named: retrieval, intermediate storage, the current goal, and suspended intentions. The mechanism for the first is the one worth carrying, because it is not a metaphor. A thing you can see is a source of activation for as long as you can see it, so it never has to be retrieved, so retrieval cannot fail on it. That gives a hard test for any support in this corpus: does the thing stay in view while the work happens, or does it appear once and go. The fourth item is the one nobody else in the corpus names. A parked goal has no home in the head, and a Return List is a place to put it. Against that, the support here is thin and secondhand: three facilitation findings from other people's studies of outlines, text networks and LISP, reported as directions with no numbers, and the paper's own seven writers contribute the observation that experienced ones already keep goal notes by hand.

rows.value: Because elements in an external representation that are perceived remain active and do not need to be retrieved, the representation can reduce retrieval failures, and it can act as a memory aid for storing the intermediate results of operations. Given the limitations of long term memory retrieval there will be many failures to retrieve goals, so an external representation of goals can be expected to help maintain them, and a representation of goals the problem solver intends to return to can be expected to help where a person must postpone an action and set an intention to deal with it later. Experienced writers already use notes of their goals to keep themselves on task.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The scarcest kind of statement in this corpus, made in 1989 and made against the paper's own interest. Everything else in the framework is a reason a representation helps; this says where the helping stops. Visibility is not learning. The support relieves retrieval by making retrieval unnecessary, and doing so builds nothing that would let the person retrieve it later on their own. That draws the line the review needs between the two questions a support has to answer, what it does for the work now and what it leaves behind, and it says the second does not follow from the first. Two cautions. The null is Craik's, about rehearsal, imported and reasoned over rather than tested here on any representation. And the authors do not sit with it: the very next move keeps a route open through chunking, and the sentence after that suggests external elements may help a reader without the schema activate one. Both are hedged as may, and neither is evidence. It is still the honest paragraph in the paper.

Thus it is unlikely that the continued activation of elements in the presence of external representations will by itself improve memory for the element. Although duration does not affect whether an element is stored, it may affect how and where it is stored, and an external representation that keeps otherwise widely separated elements in working memory may increase the likelihood that they will be stored as a unit.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: An expertise reversal written down in 1989 and never tested, and the review should carry it as a hypothesis of that vintage rather than a result. The structure that makes a novice attend to the right elements is redundant for the expert, who already attends to them, and the freer tool wins for the expert because it accepts material the structure has no slot for. That is a general shape and it recurs across this corpus. The sharper thing is in the footnote, which is where the paper puts its own undoing. The Summary Graph exists to hand novices the schema experts read with, and the footnote says novices must be taught what those elements mean and how to spot them before any of it works. So the display does not carry the meaning to the person; it gives a place to put a meaning the person must already hold. That is a precise limit on what designed structure can do on its own, and it applies to every slot-shaped support in the review.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: This is the semantic scaffolding claim proper and it answers the review's question about takeover against visibility with an example of the second kind. The empty cell removes no work from the writer. It does not find the missing position, does not fill it in, and does not know whether the source contains one. What it does is convert an absence, which is invisible in prose and in a pile of notes, into something perceptible, and then leave the writer to act. That is a mechanism worth a name, because most supports in the corpus operate on what is present. Two things make it credible as a design and not just as a phrase. The structure the writer fills was lifted from what experts were actually observed doing rather than invented, so the slots carry a claim about the task. And the authors are careful about which structure is given: three milestones are supplied, the grid's real columns are not, because discovering those is the work. Nobody was ever seen using it.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: The one place in the paper where having a representation makes the work worse, and it is the answer to the question of whether anyone here used a representation and wrote badly because of it. The finding is that committing to the finished form too early costs ideas, in both quality and quantity. That is a cost of representing, not of failing to represent, and it reframes what the other tools are for: they are not aids to writing so much as places to think that are cheap enough to abandon. The design rule that falls out is worth keeping and is rarely stated so plainly, that a support should be no more finished than the stage of work it serves. Two problems. The result is cited in a single clause with no numbers, no design and no sample, and the remedy the authors draw from it is introduced with presumably. And a page earlier the same partial product is praised for constraining what comes next, which writers are said to seek out by re-reading. Constraint helps and constraint costs, and the paper never says at what point it turns.

rows.value: To construct a finished, polished product is expensive, so we usually associate design with planning with the aid of representations and models; it is relatively expensive for a writer to produce polished formal sentences. A study by Glynn, Britton, Muth and Dogen indicated that generating polished formal sentences early in the process of writing depressed the quality and quantity of ideas that writers produced. Presumably, interactive external representations that offer writers more alternatives to formal sentences could significantly facilitate planning. Writing is also an open-ended design task in which the partially completed product becomes part of the task environment and constrains the subsequent course of the design.

items.heading: Claim 8 · CLAIM-008
items.lead: Worth carrying because it is a failure of a self-made representation rather than of a supplied one, and the corpus has almost nothing on that. The writer built the notes, the notes were the wrong notes, and there was no way to know until the work had moved past them. Two consequences follow that generalise well beyond hypertext. The first is that any staged support inherits the problem, since every stage takes the previous stage's product as its input and none of them can validate it; the paper's own chain from notes to graph to grid to tree is exactly this. The second is the design answer, which is provenance: keep a link from every abstraction to the passage it came from, so an early commitment can be checked cheaply instead of trusted. That requirement lands hard on any support that produces a summary a person will later build on without being able to see what it was made from. The evidence is seven people's protocols reported as a suggestion, and no such system was built.

rows.value: The abstractions writers make from source texts are often open to significant revision as the writer's understanding of the issue evolves, so backtracking is an architectural requirement: the system must allow users to trace information they have transformed from the original source text to notes to summary to synthesis and so on. Our case studies suggest two reasons why writers need to backtrack, to get a perspective on their current progress and to search for decisions they want to undo, and a writer will often learn that the notes and summaries taken are nonoptimal only after entering the synthesis space. Previous views do not simply inform current views; current views can also inform previous ones.
